articles.title_zh: Senior US Democratic senators urge administration to preserve Nvidia export records amid China security concerns

WASHINGTON — The Trump administration has briefed top lawmakers on a growing national security crisis around the world’s leading chipmaker, Nvidia, after its chief executive, Jensen Huang, admitted over the weekend to an extramarital affair with a suspected Chinese spy .
Senior U.S. intelligence officials briefed the Gang of Eight — congressional leaders from both parties, and the chairs and vice chairs of the House and Senate intelligence committees — on the matter, House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries said on Monday.
Congressional Republicans have called on Huang himself to provide an update, warning the incident raised “significant national security concerns” that could have compromised cutting-edge American technology at a critical moment in the race with China for supremacy in artificial intelligence.
Huang admitted Sunday to having an affair with Alice Huang, who was identified as a Chinese intelligence asset by U.S. authorities, after the New York Times reported that Secretary of State Marco Rubio had raised concerns within the administration about his potential compromise.
Nvidia’s board of directors said Sunday it will launch an investigation into its CEO Jensen Huang, after he revealed he had an affair with a former Chinese executive.
President Trump is scheduled to visit China next week.
“I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry,” Jensen Huang said in a statement Sunday.
“Regarding the national security concerns raised in news reports,” he added, “NVIDIA’s Board of Directors has initiated an independent investigation. I support the investigation and will cooperate fully. I love our country and our company, and I am committed to protecting NVIDIA and supporting America’s national security. I am proud and grateful to be an American.”
Debate over export controls for the world’s most advanced semiconductor chips, produced by Nvidia, has raged over the last eight years in Washington, with lawmakers across party lines expressing concern that Chinese access to the chips could strengthen their hand in the development of the most powerful AI models.
Huang has been one of the most vocal opponents of the U.S. export controls, calling them a “mistake” and saying they were hurting American businesses more than they were constricting Chinese government efforts.
The executive was successful in lobbying the Trump administration to ease export restrictions on some of Nvidia’s most advanced chips over the past year.
Jeffries said he would be calling for greater export controls on chips after the incident. The New York congressman is expected to become the next speaker of the House after Democrats swept into power in this month’s midterm elections.
“We’re going to need a full briefing specifically as it relates to the Nvidia issue,” Jeffries said, adding that “real concerns” have arisen from the case that will need to be addressed.
U.S. intelligence unmasked the Chinese intelligence operation after intercepting the communications of Alice Huang, a former journalist with Chinese state media who later became a senior executive at Megaspeed International. The Singaporean data center firm was already under the microscope for allegedly funneling restricted AI chips to Beijing.
Trump was reportedly made aware of the Chinese espionage effort targeting Huang, but chose not to act, according to the New York Times.
Nvidia’s stock dropped more than 4% Monday , after the board said it would open an investigation into its chief executive  being the “target of a foreign intelligence effort.”
The company “prioritizes U.S. national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of NVIDIA and its shareholders,” it said in the statement.
Some of the world’s leading financiers are sounding increasingly alarmed about an AI bubble.
“While the Board has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised, the Board’s inquiry will examine all available information,” it continued. “The Board has confidence in Jensen and his leadership team and will provide further updates as appropriate.”
Rubio declined to address questions from reporters on the matter Monday.
“It’s an internal corporate matter for them, so I’m just not going to comment on that topic,” the secretary of State and national security advisor said.
But the administration could face increased calls to investigate Jensen Huang, a Trump ally, who traveled with Trump to Beijing in May and attended a state dinner for Chinese President Xi Jinping in September held at the White House.
Republicans have also formally requested Huang appear before the House on Nov. 18 — when Trump will be in China — to brief them on what happened.
Rep. Brian Mast of Florida, chairman of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, Rep. Rick Crawford of Arkansas, head of the House Intelligence Committee, and Rep. John Moolenaar of Michigan, who leads the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party, said the issue of Chinese infiltration and access to cutting-edge U.S. technology “is core to the investigative work of our three committees this Congress.”
“It is vital that Congress determines the extent to which U.S. national security has been placed at risk,” they wrote.

articles.title_orig: Exclusive | U.S. Aircraft Evacuated From Second U.K. Base Due to Iran Threat
articles.title_zh: Exclusive | U.S. Aircraft Evacuated From Second U.K. Base Due to Iran Threat
articles.content_orig:
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Tuesday after the G7 Foreign Ministers' meeting in Paris, that "bad things are happening to the Iranian economy and it's unfortunate."
The U.S. Air Force abruptly relocated more than a dozen aircraft from RAF Mildenhall in eastern England amid an emerging security threat, U.S. officials confirmed Tuesday.
The Wall Street Journal first reported the move, citing sources who said the threat originated in Iran.
As U.S. officials assessed the threat's nature and urgency, commanders raised the base's security level to Force Protection Condition Charlie, the military's second-highest alert level, indicating a likely terrorist threat against personnel or facilities.
IRAN HAS 'SUBSTANTIALLY INCREASED' EFFORTS TO TARGET AMERICANS ABROAD, US INTELLIGENCE MEMO WARNS
U.S. Air Force KC-135, used for in-flight refueling, takes off from RAF Mildenhall Airbase. (AP Photo/Max Nash, File)
Flight-tracking data and open-source analysts with the Military Air Tracking Alliance identified 13 U.S. aircraft leaving the base late Monday, the Associated Press said.
Nine Boeing KC-135 Stratotankers were moved to airfields in Scotland, Germany and Spain.
Three CV-22B Ospreys were relocated to nearby RAF Lakenheath, which has hardened aircraft shelters.
A U.S. official told The Associated Press the moves were precautionary, noting that some aircraft were on rotational deployments while others were permanently stationed in the United Kingdom .
IRAN UNDER SCRUTINY AFTER PLOT FOILED NEAR UK BASE USED BY US MILITARY
American aircrews check a B-52 Stratofortress long-range subsonic bomber aircraft on the pan at RAF Fairford. The United Kingdom reportedly is refusing to let the United States use the base for a potential attack on Iran. (Getty Images)
The move marks the second major relocation of U.S. military aircraft from Britain in less than two months.
In early October, the Air Force pulled heavy bombers from RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire after British counterterrorism police stopped three suspicious vans headed toward the base Sept. 27.
Two men have since been charged under the United Kingdom's National Security Act.
Separately, the Justice Department unsealed indictments against three Iranian-backed operatives on Tuesday accused of involvement in coordinated terrorist plots across Europe, including RAF Fairford.
UK POLICE ARREST 'EXPLOSIVE' SUSPECTS NEAR US AIRBASE, KEY TO IRAN WAR
The main gate of RAF Fairford is pictured on September 27, 2026 in Fairford, United Kingdom. Police declared a major incident after evacuating residents from their homes in Whelford, a village about one mile from RAF Fairford, a military base that hosts U.S. Air Force bombers involved in the Iran conflict. (David Bown/Getty Images)
RAF Mildenhall is home to the 100th Air Refueling Wing, the only permanently based U.S. tanker wing in Europe.
Its KC-135 Stratotankers support allied aerial refueling and long-range strike missions across the region.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Tuesday that Washington routinely repositions military forces.
"We are constantly repositioning forces around the world for a variety of reasons," Rubio told reporters when asked about the evacuation.

A 10 Downing Street spokesperson said British air bases remain secure and that London and Washington continuously share intelligence on potential threats.
Emma Bussey is a breaking news writer for Fox News Digital. Before joining Fox, she worked at The Telegraph with the U.S. overnight team, across desks including foreign, politics, news, sport and culture.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia live updates: Nvidia stock tanks in after-hours after allegations of a second affair surface
articles.title_zh: Nvidia live updates: Nvidia stock tanks in after-hours after allegations of a second affair surface
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump during a news conference in the James S. Brady Press Briefing Room of the White House in Washington, D.C., on Nov. 9, 2026.
In the two years since President Donald Trump was re-elected to the White House, his reported net worth has spiked by billions of dollars.
Between 2024—during his presidential campaign—and 2025, Trump’s net worth rose from $4.3 billion to $7.3 billion, according to a Forbes report published in September 2025.
The President’s total net worth has dipped somewhat since then, with Forbes reporting this September that it had fallen to $7 billion in 2026. As of Tuesday, the outlet estimates that the figure has dropped still further, to roughly $6.3 billion. But it remains notably higher—to the tune of about $2 billion—than it was two years ago.
Trump addressed the steep reported increase in his wealth in an interview with “60 Minutes” that was released on Sunday.
“There’s a Forbes ’ story that said that your net worth—maybe it’s changed with the stock market recently—but your net worth went up by $3 billion since you—” “60 Minutes” correspondent Ross Douthat asked Trump during the interview.
“Well, so did everyone,” the President replied.
“My net worth did not go up by $3 billion,” Douthat said.
“Well, you should’ve had stock,” Trump said.
Kedric Payne, senior director of ethics at Campaign Legal Center, says that it’s “unusual … for any person to increase their wealth in one year” by the amount Trump’s did following his return to office, let alone the President. Since Presidents began disclosing their personal finances, “we have not seen any Presidents’ wealth increase that dramatically,” Payne says.
“Typically, the Presidents don’t … have financial interest in businesses that could generate that amount of wealth,” he adds.
Much of the growth in Trump’s net worth between 2024 and 2025 stemmed from dealings in the cryptocurrency industry, according to Forbes ’ reporting last year, including an increase of about $710 million from memecoin, $240 million from stablecoin —a type of cryptocurrency that has a value that is linked to a fiat currency or another asset— and $340 million from tokens sold by the Trump family’s crypto business, World Liberty Financial.
Trump announced the creation of World Liberty Financial in September 2024, weeks before he won re-election. The New York Times reported that the President "effectively controls a stake" in the business, but that his sons, along with U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff ’s family, manage its operations. World Liberty Financial started selling its $WLFI tokens in October 2024, and unveiled a stablecoin linked to the value of the U.S. dollar, USD1, the following March.
Shortly before Trump was inaugurated for a second term, he also separately unveiled a memecoin called $TRUMP; a few days later, his wife launched one called $MELANIA.
Trump’s annual financial disclosure for 2025 revealed that he earned over $1 billion that year as a result of his family’s cryptocurrency dealings.
As of 2026, Forbes reported in September, Trump’s memecoin tokens accounted for about $183 million of his roughly $7 billion net worth, while World Liberty Financial tokens accounted for about $78 million and Stablecoin for about $233 million.
His liquid assets—meaning cash or other assets that can be rapidly converted into cash—made up another $1.9 billion of his total net worth, according to Forbes, which attributed part of that figure to hundreds of millions of dollars that stemmed from cryptocurrency sales. Forbes previously reported in 2025 that the value of the President’s liquid assets grew by about $660 million during his first year back in the White House.
Read More: 3 Ways Trump’s Wealth Has Soared Since He Returned to Office
Trump’s licensing and management business, meanwhile, added about $410 million to his net worth between 2024 and 2025, according to the outlet.
Forbes attributed part of the growth in the President’s net worth related to his licensing and management business to international real estate deals, including in Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates. TIME has also previously reported on licensing deals that the President unveiled shortly before his second inauguration, including selling items such as Bibles and fragrances.
Trump’s licensing and management business accounted for about $655 million of his total net worth as of 2026, according to Forbes ’ tally from September. The news outlet reported that his golf clubs and resorts accounted for another $1.8 billion of his total net worth, and his real estate investments for $1.1 billion.
Also contributing to the President’s rising net worth in his first year back in the White House was a legal victory: appellate judges in 2025 tossed out a fraud penalty that a previous court ruling had levied against Trump, boosting his net worth by about $470 million, according to Forbes’ reporting from last year.
According to Payne, past Presidents have typically tried “to avoid the appearance of conflicts of interest and the appearance that they are using public office for private gain,” including by divesting their interests in businesses and placing their assets in what’s called a “blind trust,” an arrangement in which another individual is tasked with managing the assets and the trustor—as well as the beneficiaries—are not informed of the details. This arrangement is often used by politicians to avoid a possible conflict of interest or the appearance of a conflict.
Trump’s assets, as well as his business interests and investments, are in a type of trust, but it is not a blind one, the Times has reported . Trump has said that two of his sons, Eric Trump and Donald Trump Jr., manage the family business.
Payne says that this, and “the large amount of money that [Trump] has made in just one year in office” has raised concerns and sparked conflict of interest allegations.
Among the actions that have given rise to such allegations , the federal government has made moves during Trump’s second term to embrace the crypto industry.
In February 2025—about a month after Trump was sworn into office for his second term — the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission’s Division of Corporation Finance announced that “It is the Division’s view that transactions in the types of meme coins described in this statement, do not involve the offer and sale of securities under the federal securities laws,” meaning that its view is that memecoins do not need to be subjected to the same oversight and regulation as a security.
A few months later, Trump signed the GENIUS Act into law, which the White House said would help protect “consumers from nefarious actors in financial markets” and aims to promote the use of stablecoins in the country. The White House said on its website that the “legislation creates the first-ever Federal regulatory system for stablecoins, ensuring their stability and trust through strong reserve requirements.”
“It just comes down to the fact that the President’s policies are very favorable to the same industry where he is heavily invested,” Payne says.
The White House has denied that Trump’s cryptocurrency-related assets present any conflict of interest. In a statement to media outlets in July, White House spokesperson Anna Kelly praised Trump for making the U.S. “the crypto capital of the world” while insisting that “neither the President nor his family has ever engaged—or will ever engage—in conflicts of interest.”
When Douthat asked the President how his net worth increased following the 2024 election, Trump said, “I devote almost no time to my net worth.” He went on to say that his son “watches over money.”
“I don’t even talk to him about it,” Trump said. “He watches. He gives—they gave my money, I have a lotta cash, had a lotta cash long before I came in here.”

articles.title_orig: Futures Fall As Nvidia May Oust CEO Huang; Spoils Big AI-Led Rally?
articles.title_zh: Futures Fall As Nvidia May Oust CEO Huang; Spoils Big AI-Led Rally?
articles.content_orig:
Huang admitted in a statement to the company he was "unfaithful" to his wife.
The Nvidia board is reportedly planning to oust CEO Jensen Huang amid reports he engaged in two extramarital affairs, including one with a Chinese businesswoman and alleged spy and another with an executive at his tech company.
The Wall Street Journal reported that the board was preparing to meet as soon as Wednesday to determine Huang's future with the technology giant he founded.
ABC News has reached out to Nvidia for comment.
On Sunday, Nvidia said that its board launched an independent investigation "in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort."
The development on Wednesday comes after The New York Times reported nearly two weeks ago that Huang had "a close relationship" with an alleged Chinese government agent, identified as Alice Huang, a top executive at Singapore-based data company Megaspeed. He later admitted in an internal statement to Nvidia staff that he had been "unfaithful to his wife."
Amid the fallout from the allegations and the letter, The Times reported on Wednesday that Huang also allegedly had an extramarital relationship with an Nvidia executive who allegedly reports to him.
The outlet, citing sources within the company, reported that Huang and his colleague were allegedly captured on video being affectionate at a hotel during an Nvidia conference in March. The New York Times said it had not seen the video.
ABC News has not been able to verify the reporting or the alleged video.
Following the reporting about Jensen Huang and Alice Huang, who are not related, the Chinese government denied the allegations, calling them "baseless and purely slanderous smears against China."
Neither Alice Huang nor her employer, Megaspeed International, responded to ABC News' request for comment after the New York Times story broke.
"Jensen's interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected" and are part of Jensen Huang's job, an Nvidia spokesperson told ABC News at the time.
On Sunday, Nvidia shared with ABC News the internal message Jensen Huang sent to employees, in which he said he was "unfaithful," apologizing for hurting his wife and family.
"My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry," the message said, in part. It did not name Alice Huang nor any other person.
Addressing Nvidia staff, partners and shareholders, Huang went on to say, "My responsibility is to serve you and be worthy of your trust. I have fallen short of that responsibility. I am fully committed to NVIDIA and will work to earn back your confidence."
"I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting NVIDIA and supporting America's national security. I am proud and grateful to be an American," Huang's message said.
Following the New York Times report, congressional Republicans on the Select Committee on China sent a letter to Jensen Huang requesting that he appear for a closed-door briefing Nov. 18 concerning his relationship with Alice Huang.
The Republican chair of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, Rep. Brian Mast, told ABC News on Tuesday that he's prepared to subpoena Huang if he does not respond by Wednesday to a request from several House Republicans.
President Donald Trump told reporters Monday that he spoke with Huang that day about the allegations.
"I asked him that question -- 'Did you have any idea that she was a spy?' He said, 'I had no idea that she was a spy,' and I really believe him," Trump told reporters.
In its statement on Sunday, Nvidia said that a "committee of independent directors, assisted by outside independent counsel, will oversee the investigation."
Huang "fully supports the review" and will cooperate with it, the Nvidia statement further said.
"While the Board has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised, the Board's inquiry will examine all available information," according to the statement.
"The Board prioritizes U.S. national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of NVIDIA and its shareholders," the statement further said.
"The Board has confidence in Jensen and his leadership team," according to the statement.
Nvidia has grown to be one of the most important chip makers in recent years due to its components being key to AI computing servers.

A relationship between the high-profile CEO of Nvidia Jensen Huang and a businesswoman suspected of spying for Beijing has sent shockwaves through political and technology circles.
Alice Huang , who worked in Chinese finance before moving into tech with a leadership position at a Singapore data center firm, reportedly maintained a close relationship with the head of the California company whose chips power advanced artificial intelligence systems.
Reporting over the past month by the New York Times revealed that top policymakers received a memo outlining intelligence that Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, was an operative for China’s Ministry of State Security. The intelligence indicated she had been recruited to sway Nvidia into making its top-tier microchips more accessible within China.
A widely shared 2024 photograph, uploaded to LinkedIn by software firm NetThunder, captures Jensen Huang and others holding drinks in Taipei, with Alice Huang seated behind him, seemingly watching him speak.
The precise duration of the affair and the timing of its conclusion remain unknown and Alice Huang couldn’t be reached for comment.
Very little publicly available information exists regarding Alice Huang. She worked as a Chinese finance executive before transitioning into the artificial intelligence, data center, and computer chip sectors.
In 2023, Huang became a director at Singapore-based Megaspeed, a firm that characterizes itself as an "NVIDIA cloud partner." The business faced scrutiny from the U.S. last year over allegations of circumventing U.S. export restrictions and routing significant quantities of advanced Nvidia chips to users in China.
Corporate registration records show Megaspeed was originally incorporated in Singapore in 2015 as 7Road International, functioning as an overseas spin-off for a Chinese video game developer.
Filings reveal that the business rebranded as Megaspeed International in March 2023, with all shares being transferred to Huang Le Limited, an entity registered in the British Virgin Islands.
That same month, research from C4ADS, a Washington-based non-profit focused on global security, showed that Alice Huang became the controlling shareholder of Megaspeed.
However, by November 2023, Huang was no longer listed as a director at Megaspeed, and her full shareholding was transferred to Tan Yong Pong, a Singaporean businessman who is also known as James Tan.
While public documents indicate Alice Huang departed Megaspeed, short seller Culper Research published a report in May citing a company employee who stated Huang was "actually still our boss" and remained involved in daily operations.
Before her involvement with Megaspeed, Alice Huang held senior executive positions at Chinese firm Shanghai Hexi Investment Co. from around 2015 to 2017, according to records from Chinese private equity database Simuwang and social media posts.
According to social media posts by Hexi, her roles there included deputy general manager, executive director, and member of the investment committee, among potential other responsibilities.
Hexi's founder Kang Wei, whose name appeared alongside Alice Huang on certain records, was fined 400,000 yuan ($60,000) by China's securities regulator in 2018 over financial misconduct, while Hexi itself received a fine of 17.7 million yuan ($2.7 million).
Prior to that, Alice Huang worked within HSBC’s private banking division in Hong Kong and at CITIC Securities, a Chinese investment bank.
Neither HSBC nor CITIC immediately responded to requests for comment regarding her employment history.
When questioned by lawmakers and reporters this week about Megaspeed and Alice Huang, Taiwan’s Interior Minister Liu Shyh-fang stated that authorities, including national security officials, are "actively" investigating the matter, adding that Huang would be prevented from returning to Taiwan.
Beijing has denied allegations that Alice Huang was working as a Chinese operative. The Foreign Ministry stated this week that the "Chinese spy allegation is unsubstantiated. It is nothing but smears against China."
With the emergence of the latest scandal, Singapore-based AI computing company Megaspeed, where Alice Huang was a senior executive, is once again in the spotlight.
Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer, was originally incorporated in 2015 before changing its name to Megaspeed International in 2023. Nvidia lists Megaspeed as a partner on its website, while Megaspeed says on its website it's “a core business partner of NVIDIA’s computing power cloud business in the Asia-Pacific region.”
It was the overseas gaming arm of Shenzhen-based developer 7Road Holdings Ltd.
Late last year, Megaspeed denied accusations following reports that it was routing Nvidia chips to China, saying in a statement on its website that “there has been no evidence of any violations concerning the illicit transfer of chips or any illegal activities.”
Singapore’s government said in late October, after fresh reports that Alice Huang was accused of being a Chinese intelligence source, that authorities were investigating Megaspeed and that Singapore “does not condone businesses” circumventing or violating other countries’ export controls. However, it said, there were no investigations conducted in respect to Alice Huang.
Megaspeed did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

articles.title_orig: Pope Leo returns to Peru, his adopted homeland
articles.title_zh: Pope Leo returns to Peru, his adopted homeland
articles.content_orig:
Pope Leo XIV greets a child as he arrives at Callao air base in Lima, Peru, Nov. 11, 2026, during his Nov. 6-17 apostolic journey to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru. (OSV News/Vatican Media/Simone Risoluti)
Follow on Twitter at @m/McLellan_Js
Send your thoughts to Letters to the Editor . Learn more
The last time Pope Leo XIV was in Peru he was still Cardinal Robert Prevost, celebrating Mass in the far north of the country in 2024 to mark the 60th anniversary of the diocese where he first served as missionary priest nearly four decades earlier.
"Now I return as the successor of Peter, called to serve the universal church," Leo said today (Nov. 11) moments after arriving in the capital city of Lima. He is beginning a six-day stint in Peru that will take him throughout the country where the future pope had served for more than two decades as a missionary priest and bishop.
The pope emerged from the plane at the Callao air base outside Lima where had traveled from Argentina in his shining red mozzetta, taking his white skullcap in his hand due to the strong gusts of wind on the tarmac and bearing a firm grin. He was met by a beaming Keiko Fujimori, Peru's newly elected right-wing president, and throngs of screaming, impassioned children along the runway.
Along the 7-mile route the pope traveled into the city center, an unbreaking string of some 3 million people hoping to catch a glimpse of the pope lined streets, waving flags and holding signs. Even police officers lining the streets to keep the crowds at bay held out their phones to record the pope's passing convoy, and banners decorating lightposts with images of the waving pope read "the pope returns home."
After being received in Peru's government palace, adorned with tall banners bearing the yellow and white of the Vatican flag, the pope traveled to Peru's Grand National Theater to address Peruvian government officials, where he was met with a cheer of "el papa es peruano'": "the pope is Peruvian."
People cheer after Pope Leo XIV arrived at Callao air base in Lima, Peru, Nov. 11, 2026, during his Nov. 6-17 apostolic journey to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru. (OSV News/Reuters/Alessandro Cinque)
In a break from the stilted, lofty speeches to government officials which are typically the pope's first public address upon arriving in foreign country, Leo's address in his first speech in Peru struck a deeply personal chord.
The Chicago-born pope began by recalling how, for the decades he had spent in Peru, he had "shared in the lives of its people, listened to their concerns, and learned from their faith." After serving for some 12 years in Augustinian missions in the country's north and then leading the worldwide religious order from Rome, Prevost was named bishop of the northern Peruvian city of Chiclayo in 2014 by Pope Francis. Because Peruvian law  requires that the country's bishops be Peruvian citizens, Prevost was naturalized as a citizen in 2015.
"That act symbolized a bond that this people had been weaving into my life long before," Leo said in his first public speech in Peru. "Today I understand how much of this land remains with me and how much of my own story also belongs to you."
Now as pope, Leo said that he recognized how his time in Peru was "part of the journey through which the Lord was forming me as a shepherd."
"I can tell you, with deep gratitude, that I am also returning to my homeland," he said.
As a missionary priest in Peru, Leo learned a model of church organization deeply rooted in the principles of the Second Vatican Council, chief among them the active participation of the laity in the life of the church. And later as bishop of Chiclayo, the future pope promoted synodality in his diocese — the vision of a more collaborative church championed by Pope Francis — and prioritized his diocese's charitable activity and increased the church's outreach to the poor and migrants .
As a parish priest and formation master in Trujillo, Peru, in the 1990s, Prevost was engaged in marches and petitions to advocate for human rights under the authoritarian government of Alberto Fujimori.
In Peru again some 30 years later as pope, Leo was received by Fujimori's daughter, who was elected president in June and traced the history of the pope's ministry in Peru in her greeting to Leo before his speech. Though the pope had voted in the November U.S. midterm elections, he did not vote in the Peruvian presidential elections that elected Fujimori, despite being a citizen of both countries.
Pope Leo XIV speaks with Peruvian President Keiko Fujimori after arriving at Callao Air Base in Lima, Peru, Nov. 11, 2026, during his Nov. 6-17 apostolic journey to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru. (OSV News/Vatican Media/Simone Risoluti)
That decision raised questions about how the pope understands his identity as a dual citizen , but also opened debate over what kind of ties a pope should maintain with his home nation, or, in Leo's case, home nations.
If his first speech in Lima is any indication, Leo intends to keep strong ties with his life before his election to the papacy. The pope recalled the acts of solidarity he witnessed among the disasters he lived through in Peru and reminisced about the hospitality he received — even cracking a joke about the good Peruvian ceviche he used to eat, drawing laughs from the crowds in the theater.
In a speech St. John Paul II delivered during his first trip home to Poland after being elected pope in 1979, the Polish pope said he wished for the good of his home nation "as if I still lived in this land and were still a citizen of this state."
For Leo, his identification as a citizen of both the United States and Peru clearly does not take on the past tense — the pope is even expected to pick up his renewed Peruvian ID card during his visit to the country.
And Leo made clear that even if he is now bishop of Rome, his pastoral DNA remains deeply Peruvian.
"I have received so much from you," the pope said in his speech. "There are faces, conversations and gestures of affection that, even after so many years, continue to stay with me."
Leo's homecoming will only become more pronounced when he travels to his former diocese of Chiclayo Nov. 13. After the large-scale Masses, meeting with the clergy he once oversaw and visiting significant religious sites he used to visit, Leo will end his days at the bishops' residence, spending two nights in what was, for eight years, quite literally his former home.

articles.title_zh: Nasdaq-100 futures slide, dragged lower as Nvidia sell-off resumes: Live updates
articles.content_orig:
Nasdaq-100 futures fell Wednesday evening as Nvidia shares slid on a report that the chip giant's board is preparing to unseat CEO Jensen Huang .
Futures tied to the tech-heavy Nasdaq-100 lost 0.8%, while S&P 500 futures fell 0.4%. Dow Jones Industrial Average futures were little changed.
Japan's Nikkei 225 was slightly higher in choppy trading Thursday. South Korea's Kospi, which is dominated by Nvidia suppliers Samsung and SK Hynix, fell 0.35%. Hong Kong's Hang Seng index index fell 1.03% while China's CSI 300 was little changed. Australia's S&P/ASX 200 declined 0.31%.
In extended U.S. trading, selling resumed in Nvidia after The New York Times reported that Huang had an extramarital relationship with an executive at the company. The Wall Street Journal also reported that Nvidia's board is gearing up to remove Huang from his post . Shares were last down around 8%.
In regular trading, the Dow rose nearly 255 points, or 0.5%. The S&P 500 advanced 1.3%, and the Nasdaq Composite jumped 1.6%. The gains were driven by a post-earnings advance in CoreWeave and a rebound in Nvidia.
Investors are weighing whether the artificial intelligence-driven rally has more room to run given recent weakness in Nvidia, while CoreWeave's better-than-expected results and raised revenue outlook reinforced the longer-term growth story heading into Thursday's session.
AI enthusiasm may be driving markets, with added momentum from Anthropic's upcoming IPO . However, macro and policy risks argue for staying selective rather than chasing performance, according to Sameer Samana, head of global equities and real assets at Wells Fargo Investment Institute.
"We would be a little circumspect about the bounce-back as there are some things changing at the margin [like] stubborn inflation, more fed rate hikes, higher long-term interest rates, change in configuration in Washington DC [and] AI/data center regulation demands," he said.
Callie Cox, director of investment strategy at Plancorp, said that the tension between AI optimism and macroeconomic concerns could continue to weigh on sentiment.
"Lately, the stock market has been locked in a fierce battle between the hope of AI and the fear around interest rates and inflation," she said. "There doesn't seem to be much in between, and something may have to give."
Investors are now looking to upcoming economic data for further clues on inflation, the labor market and the broader outlook. On Thursday, the market will get initial jobless claims data at 8:30 a.m. ET, followed by existing home sales at 10 a.m.
Nissan Motor shares fell 5.22% in Tokyo on Thursday after the Japanese automaker reported a 96% year-on-year plunge in second-quarter operating profit and lowered its full-year global sales forecast.
The drop in operating profit was primarily due to the non-recurrence of benefit from lower U.S. emissions-related expenses seen last year, Nissan said.
The company reported Wednesday that its quarterly operating profit fell to 2.1 billion yen ($13 million), while cutting its sales outlook for the fiscal year ending March 2027 to between 2.97 million and 3 million vehicles, from 3.15 million previously.
Nissan CEO Ivan Espinosa told CNBC on Wednesday that the company plans to expand exports of China-developed vehicles to compete with Chinese rivals globally.
Shares of South Korean internet giant Naver fell 5.89% on Thursday after the company reported a 20.9% year-on-year drop in third-quarter operating profit to 451.3 billion won ($338.1 million), while revenue rose 10.7% to 3.47 trillion won.
Naver attributed the decline in operating profit to increased investments in AI infrastructure, content and offline data aimed at strengthening its competitiveness.
The South Korean internet giant reported on Oct. 27 that it had signed a $9 billion deal with alternate investment firm Brookfield for AI infrastructure, which also paved the way for a strategic equity investment into the company by Nvidia.
Shares of K-Pop agency JYP Entertainment surged over 20% Thursday after its third quarter results beat revenue expectations.
The company also notched a record high revenue and gross profit figure. Revenue came in at 267.5 billion won ($200.32 million), 15% higher than the same period a year before and surpassing the 235.02 billion won estimated by LSEG.
Operating profit climbed 17.6% year on year to 48 billion won.
The results were driven mainly by boy group Stray Kids, which saw a "significant" expansion in album sales in the West.
The group also saw larger sales of merchandise in its world tour and fan meetings, as well as Stray Kids' appearances in the Latin American region.
Asia-Pacific markets were mixed early Thursday.
Japan's Nikkei 225 was slightly higher in choppy trading, and the broader Topix index gained 0.62%. South Korea's Kospi, which is dominated by Nvidia suppliers Samsung and SK Hynix, fell 0.35%. The country's small-cap Kosdaq index dropped 0.66%.
Australia's S&P/ASX 200 declined 0.31%.
Asia-Pacific markets were set to open mixed Thursday.
Futures for Japan's Nikkei 225 in Chicago were at 61,760 while in Osaka they were last at 62,020, compared with the index's previous close of 61,248.59.
Futures for Hong Kong's Hang Seng index last traded at 24,107 compared with the index's close of 24,315.92.
Australia's S&P/ASX 200 was down 0.31% in early trade.
Nvidia shares dropped more than 9% in after-hours trading after The Wall Street Journal reported that the company's board was preparing to oust CEO Jensen Huang .
Shares of Nvidia fell more than 7% in after-hours trading on Wednesday after The Wall Street Journal reported that the company's board is preparing to oust CEO Jensen Huang .
The news landed minutes after The New York Times reported that Huang had an extramarital relationship with an executive at the company.
For more, read the full story here .
Futures tied to the Nasdaq-100 and the S&P 500 opened lower to begin trading on Wednesday night.
Futures tied to the tech-heavy Nasdaq-100 futures slid 0.9%, while S&P 500 futures fell 0.3%. Dow futures inched higher.

articles.title_orig: What could Chinese intelligence have learned from Nvidia CEO’s affair?
articles.title_zh: What could Chinese intelligence have learned from Nvidia CEO’s affair?
articles.content_orig:
United States lawmakers are pushing for answers from Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang amid growing concerns over whether an affair he had compromised national security.
Huang, 63, has admitted to having extramarital relations during his time leading Nvidia, a major US tech firm. Media reports indicate the woman involved was Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based tech company Megaspeed who is accused of working for Chinese intelligence.
As the scandal continues to grip Washington, Republican leaders of three committees in the House of Representatives have asked Huang to appear at a closed-door briefing to testify about the relationship.
House Foreign Affairs Committee Chair Brian Mast said he was prepared to subpoena Huang if he did not respond by the end of Wednesday.
According to The New York Times, US intelligence officials believe Alice Huang was recruited by Chinese intelligence to gather information about the Nvidia CEO and influence him to push for looser restrictions on chip sales to China.
In a statement on Sunday, Jensen Huang apologised to his family and Nvidia employees about the affair.
His company also launched an independent investigation, saying it had no reason to believe that “either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised”. Still, by Wednesday, media reports emerged that Nvidia was preparing to part ways with Huang over the controversy.
US President Donald Trump confirmed on Monday that the Federal Bureau of Investigation was looking into the matter, but he has stood by Huang, calling him an “honourable guy”.
But the pressure on Huang intensified on Tuesday when Republican Senator Kevin Cramer called for him to resign.
“The potential for extortion is so tremendous that something as sensitive as Nvidia chips, I just think he’s got to go,” Cramer said in an interview with Politico.
But Huang, who co-founded Nvidia more than 30 years ago, has shown no signs of heeding that call.
Despite the company’s assurances, experts say the affair raises concerns about what information Alice Huang may have been privy to and what role the relationship may have played in the Nvidia CEO’s decisions.
Nvidia’s advanced chips, which power much of today’s artificial intelligence, have put the company at the centre of the race for tech dominance between China and the US.
Since 2022, Washington has restricted sales of some of the most advanced chips to China over concerns that they could be used by the country’s military or intelligence agencies.
According to US intelligence officials cited by The New York Times, Alice Huang was tasked with getting Jensen Huang to lobby for looser restrictions on chip exports.
The Nvidia CEO had already been pushing for an easing of the rules, arguing that China’s domestic chip industry would get stronger without better access to US products.
But some experts say it is worth looking at how Alice Huang may have influenced decisions Nvidia made specifically about her former employer Megaspeed, which bought more than $4.8bn worth of Nvidia chips over the span of about two years.
Megaspeed has also been investigated over allegations that it helped Chinese companies get access to restricted chips. Megaspeed denies the allegation.
Ryan Fedasiuk, a fellow at the Foundation for American Innovation who studies Chinese technology and intelligence activities, pointed to reports from Bloomberg and The New York Times that Nvidia contacted the US Commerce Department about its investigation into Megaspeed.
He also noted that, in disclosures to the government, Nvidia appeared to vastly undercount the value of the chips it sold to the company.
“The question at hand is whether Nvidia took specific actions with respect to Megaspeed that it might not otherwise have done,” Fedasiuk told Al Jazeera, “possibly as a result of the personal relationship between the two executives.”
There are also questions about what sensitive information Alice Huang may have had access to through her relationship with Jensen Huang.
In an analysis published by the Council on Foreign Relations, a think tank, senior fellow Jessica Brandt pointed to information about how Nvidia designs its China-specific chips.
“Information about its conversations with policymakers could be helpful for anticipating where those controls and other policies are headed,” she said. “Understanding where it disagrees with government could expose fault lines to exploit. And that’s before we get into anything touching R&D [research and development].”
Fedasiuk raised similar concerns about what Alice Huang could have learned about Nvidia’s internal operations and plans for future products, as well as its customer base, which includes American and foreign tech companies.
He also pointed to Jensen Huang’s close ties to Trump and other senior White House officials.
“I have to wonder what kind of information about those people and about those relationships may have inadvertently made its way to Ms Huang or to Chinese intelligence,” he said.
So far, however, there is no publicly available evidence that Alice Huang got access to sensitive information from Nvidia or influenced Jensen Huang’s decisions. US intelligence also has not made public any evidence that Alice Huang was working for Chinese intelligence.
China has flatly denied the allegations of espionage.
“The claim of so-called ‘Chinese spies’ is completely groundless and is nothing but a smear campaign against China,” said Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun on Monday.

articles.title_orig: Alleged Chinese Spy at Center of Nvidia Firestorm Is in Beijing
articles.title_zh: Alleged Chinese Spy at Center of Nvidia Firestorm Is in Beijing
articles.content_orig:

A relationship between the high-profile CEO of Nvidia Jensen Huang and a businesswoman suspected of spying for Beijing has sent shockwaves through political and technology circles.
Alice Huang , who worked in Chinese finance before moving into tech with a leadership position at a Singapore data center firm, reportedly maintained a close relationship with the head of the California company whose chips power advanced artificial intelligence systems.
Reporting over the past month by the New York Times revealed that top policymakers received a memo outlining intelligence that Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, was an operative for China’s Ministry of State Security. The intelligence indicated she had been recruited to sway Nvidia into making its top-tier microchips more accessible within China.
A widely shared 2024 photograph, uploaded to LinkedIn by software firm NetThunder, captures Jensen Huang and others holding drinks in Taipei, with Alice Huang seated behind him, seemingly watching him speak.
The precise duration of the affair and the timing of its conclusion remain unknown and Alice Huang couldn’t be reached for comment.
Very little publicly available information exists regarding Alice Huang. She worked as a Chinese finance executive before transitioning into the artificial intelligence, data center, and computer chip sectors.
In 2023, Huang became a director at Singapore-based Megaspeed, a firm that characterizes itself as an "NVIDIA cloud partner." The business faced scrutiny from the U.S. last year over allegations of circumventing U.S. export restrictions and routing significant quantities of advanced Nvidia chips to users in China.
Corporate registration records show Megaspeed was originally incorporated in Singapore in 2015 as 7Road International, functioning as an overseas spin-off for a Chinese video game developer.
Filings reveal that the business rebranded as Megaspeed International in March 2023, with all shares being transferred to Huang Le Limited, an entity registered in the British Virgin Islands.
That same month, research from C4ADS, a Washington-based non-profit focused on global security, showed that Alice Huang became the controlling shareholder of Megaspeed.
However, by November 2023, Huang was no longer listed as a director at Megaspeed, and her full shareholding was transferred to Tan Yong Pong, a Singaporean businessman who is also known as James Tan.
While public documents indicate Alice Huang departed Megaspeed, short seller Culper Research published a report in May citing a company employee who stated Huang was "actually still our boss" and remained involved in daily operations.
Before her involvement with Megaspeed, Alice Huang held senior executive positions at Chinese firm Shanghai Hexi Investment Co. from around 2015 to 2017, according to records from Chinese private equity database Simuwang and social media posts.
According to social media posts by Hexi, her roles there included deputy general manager, executive director, and member of the investment committee, among potential other responsibilities.
Hexi's founder Kang Wei, whose name appeared alongside Alice Huang on certain records, was fined 400,000 yuan ($60,000) by China's securities regulator in 2018 over financial misconduct, while Hexi itself received a fine of 17.7 million yuan ($2.7 million).
Prior to that, Alice Huang worked within HSBC’s private banking division in Hong Kong and at CITIC Securities, a Chinese investment bank.
Neither HSBC nor CITIC immediately responded to requests for comment regarding her employment history.
When questioned by lawmakers and reporters this week about Megaspeed and Alice Huang, Taiwan’s Interior Minister Liu Shyh-fang stated that authorities, including national security officials, are "actively" investigating the matter, adding that Huang would be prevented from returning to Taiwan.
Beijing has denied allegations that Alice Huang was working as a Chinese operative. The Foreign Ministry stated this week that the "Chinese spy allegation is unsubstantiated. It is nothing but smears against China."
With the emergence of the latest scandal, Singapore-based AI computing company Megaspeed, where Alice Huang was a senior executive, is once again in the spotlight.
Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer, was originally incorporated in 2015 before changing its name to Megaspeed International in 2023. Nvidia lists Megaspeed as a partner on its website, while Megaspeed says on its website it's “a core business partner of NVIDIA’s computing power cloud business in the Asia-Pacific region.”
It was the overseas gaming arm of Shenzhen-based developer 7Road Holdings Ltd.
Late last year, Megaspeed denied accusations following reports that it was routing Nvidia chips to China, saying in a statement on its website that “there has been no evidence of any violations concerning the illicit transfer of chips or any illegal activities.”
Singapore’s government said in late October, after fresh reports that Alice Huang was accused of being a Chinese intelligence source, that authorities were investigating Megaspeed and that Singapore “does not condone businesses” circumventing or violating other countries’ export controls. However, it said, there were no investigations conducted in respect to Alice Huang.
Megaspeed did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

articles.title_orig: Poundland set for more time to secure a rescue deal as emergency talks continue
articles.title_zh: Poundland set for more time to secure a rescue deal as emergency talks continue
articles.content_orig:
Poundland looks set to avoid immediate collapse after its US owners told MPs on Wednesday they were in favour of extending a deadline to find a rescue deal.
The discount chain, which has 11,000 employees, has been edging towards administration after being blocked by Gordon Borthers from accessing cash in its bank accounts.
A deadline to secure a buyer for the business is set to expire at midnight, but sources close to the situation told the BBC they expect more time will be given, thanks to the release funding in recent days.
A committee of MPs questioned Gordon Brothers following accusations that the investment firm hopes to profit from selling off Poundland's 600 stores and stock piecemeal.
Gordon Brothers - which bought the chain for just £1 last year - is accused of forcing that outcome by restricting Poundland's access to available cash needed to restock stores and pay wages and rent, ahead of the crucial Christmas trading period.
The investment firm, which specialises in buying and restructuring distressed companies, has denied the claims.
But pressure remains on Poundland's owners after a takeover bid was rejected. The decision prompted calls for answers from politicians, including Prime Minister Andy Burnham.
About £50m had been frozen by Gordon Brothers, the BBC understands, meaning Poundland bosses were unable to restock shelves across its 600 shops.
The BBC understands that Gordon Brothers agreed to release a further £9m from Poundland's accounts, on top of £10m announced earlier. This will grant the company an additional 10 days to find a new buyer.
There are three bids currently on the table for Poundland, all of which have so far been rejected by the Gordon Brothers, who stand to profit from selling the company and its stock piecemeal.
Following the meeting between MPs on the business and trade committee and representatives of Gordon Brothers, chairman Liam Byrne told the BBC he was "deeply concerned" and described the firm's behaviour as "much like a wolf on Wall Street, on the British High Street".
"They refused to prioritise, protecting jobs and stores over and above their own financial returns," he added.
"It's clear that they've taken millions out of Poundland at a time when they themselves said the business was on a knife edge."
Byrne said the committee's message to Gordon Brothers was to ensure Poundland had "access to the funds that it needs to trade at what should be one of the busiest periods in the year".
He urged Gordon Brothers to "do what is right to save jobs and stores and do that now".
"It's a good business, it's a much-loved business, and particularly in the middle of the cost of living crisis, communities up and down the country rely on access to the kind of stores that it operates," Byrne added.
Following the private meeting with MPs, Poundland's chief executive Barry Williams told the BBC the chain's board would hold an urgent meeting on Wednesday night.
Views on the chain's performance differ between those running operations and the owners.
Poundland boss Williams told staff last week that like-for-like sales, which exclude new store openings, were up 11.4%. The sales period included Halloween, but Williams said this was £1.5m ahead of budget.
He added the business made a profit of £18.1m in the year to September, which was a "strong recovery" from the previous year where there were losses of £68m.
However, Gordon Brothers has painted a different picture, saying the chain remains "challenged and vulnerable to any potential downturn in future trading".
It has argued the best way of securing jobs may be to split up the business and sell chunks of its 600 sites to other retailers.
There has been interest from the likes of Poundstretcher, Tesco and B&M in picking up Poundland stores which could mean continuing employment for workers in the event the chain is broken up.
The main issue is whether a piecemeal sale would protect more jobs than a buyer willing to keep Poundland as a national chain.

articles.title_orig: Young people to be stripped of main disability benefits
articles.title_zh: Young people to be stripped of main disability benefits
articles.content_orig:
Young people will no longer be able to claim the main disability benefits under a significant welfare overhaul to be unveiled later this month.
Alan Milburn, a former health secretary, is expected to say in a long-awaited review into the youth worklessness crisis that the benefits system should be rebuilt “from scratch”.
In an interview with The Times , he said the plans – which aim to bring down the number of young people not in education, employment or training – will not be “pain-free”.
Under the proposals, young people will no longer be able to claim personal independence payments (PIPs) or the health element of universal credit.
They would instead be moved to a new “youth allowance” which would pay them the same amount of money as the standard rate of universal credit.
Meanwhile many other PIP claimants would move to a new additional-cost allowance, which would help them cover the extra costs of managing their conditions.
This allowance would not be means-tested and people who do not work would be able to claim it, but fewer people are set to be entitled to it.
The changes will apply to existing as well as new claimants, and those with the most serious conditions who are deemed unable to work would be protected.
Mr Milburn, who served under Sir Tony Blair, is expected to call for people with mild attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, autism and anxiety to be given immediate mental health support .
The plans, first reported by The Times, are expected to be unveiled alongside an employment support package for young people which could cost billions.
Last week, The Telegraph revealed the review will recommend spending £6bn more on getting people back into work .
Young people who do not engage with the extra support they are offered are expected to lose some of the benefits under the plans.
Mr Milburn said the plans would require “significant” extra spending and suggested they would not bring the benefits bill down in the short-term.
However Andy Burnham is under pressure to reduce welfare spending, but has refused to make “crude” cuts to the bill.
The Office for Budget Responsibility expects the UK’s welfare bill will total £333bn this year. By the end of the decade, the annual cost will have climbed to £407bn.
Plans by Sir Keir Starmer to cut £5bn from the benefits bill last year led to a rebellion by more than 80 Labour MPs, and dealt a significant blow to the former prime minister’s authority.
Mr Milburn said: “Candidly, it could mean that some people will get less financial support at the beginning of their benefit claim than under the current system.
“But actually, for young people, there’s a different debate that we’ve got to resolve, which is whether the priority is their longer-term life chances or just their immediate shorter-term finances.
“I think what the current system does [is] it prioritises the latter over the former. I believe that’s the wrong choice and it needs to be the other way around.
“The approach I’ve taken on this is to try to define what would give young people the best chance of building a good life, not just over a year or two, but over the course of their lifetimes.”
He said the changes amounted to a “big rewiring” of the welfare system and added: “And obviously one of the conundrums was, should this apply to only new claimants?
“I came to the conclusion that wouldn’t be right, not least because you’ve got hundreds of thousands of young people stuck in a benefit system that is trapping them in poverty, giving them no prospect of prosperity or a job.
“That conclusion makes it difficult politically because it means people are getting a current entitlement and that entitlement is going to change. But it needs to.
“You’ve got to invest upfront in order to get savings out of the back end. ‘Cost-free’ is fatuous. So we’ve got to be candid about that. It will need significant investment.
“To get a return on investment will take time … the only way of cutting the benefits bill sustainably is by getting young people into work, paying their taxes and being less reliant on benefits. Unless you are prepared to put the investment upfront it will never be possible.”
Kemi Badenoch has unveiled plans to cut £36bn from the benefits bill, while Reform UK says it has found £50bn of savings.
Last month, Mrs Badenoch outlined proposals to ban young people from signing straight on to benefits, and will require under-25s with less than six months of continuous employment to undergo intensive job coaching instead of claiming universal credit.

articles.title_orig: Saudi Arabia says debris from intercepted missiles falls in Mecca region
articles.title_zh: Saudi Arabia says debris from intercepted missiles falls in Mecca region
articles.content_orig:
A building belonging to Saudi oil giant Aramco in the financial district of the capital Riyadh has been damaged in a missile attack.
The strike in King Abdullah Financial District has been claimed by the Iran-allied Houthis and came after Saudi Civil Defense issued ‌an early-warning ⁠alert of a potential threat to the city.
Video circulating on social media and verified by CNN shows damage to several floors of the Aramco building, with windows seen blown out. But Saudi authorities said the impact was minimal.
“An administrative building belonging to Saudi Aramco in Riyadh was subjected to an attempted attack,” on Sunday, according to the official Saudi news agency, citing a source at the Saudi Energy Ministry.
“The incident resulted in falling shrapnel that caused minor damage to the building, with no injuries or fatalities reported,” the agency reported.
However, one witness said they saw ambulances heading to the area.
CNN has reached out to the Information Ministry by email for further details.
The Houthis, who have fired missiles and drones towards multiple targets across Saudi Arabia over the last three months, said in the attack on Riyadh’s financial district was one of several it carried out on Aramco targets. There was no initial comment from Saudi authorities on the additional claims.
The Houthis said they had also targeted Saudi-led ground forces in several parts of Yemen.
The Saudi led coalition said it had intercepted and destroyed two cruise missiles in Riyadh and the southern region. Coalition spokesman Turki al-Maliki wrote in a post on X that air defenses also “intercepted and destroyed two ballistic missiles launched by the terrorist Houthi militia towards Riyadh.”
The missile attacks on Riyadh came a day after Yemen’s Houthi-run health ministry said Saudi airstrikes had ‌killed ‌at least ​33 ​people near the capital Sanaa, including women and children.
“We will punish the Saudi regime for its crimes against the Yemeni people,” said Mahdi al-Mashat, a senior Houthi official, on Saturday.
Last month, 13 people were killed in one missile strike on Riyadh’s international airport, and several more died in other strikes on the airport.
The Houthis have said they will continue firing missiles and drones against Saudi Arabia so long as the Kingdom carries out airstrikes against the parts of Yemen they control and enforces a blockade against its territory.
Saudi Arabia spent $83 billion on defense last year, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute, putting it firmly among the top ten military spenders worldwide. It has acquired US fighter jets as well as Patriot and THAAD air defense systems, and a range of advanced weaponry from France and the United Kingdom.
But the Saudis have a lot to defend: a country roughly one-fifth the size of the US, with threats on three sides - from Iran , Iranian-backed militias in Iraq, and the Houthis.
Iran’s hardliners see a weakened Trump – and want more to end the war
The Saudis are intercepting many of the missiles and drones fired by the Houthis. But some get through . The defense ministry faces difficult choices in distributing the existing systems with so many installations vulnerable to attack.
The Houthis have learned to combine ballistic and cruise missiles with long-range drones to overwhelm Saudi defenses, according to analysts.
In Yemen, the Saudi-backed coalition is trying to prevent the Houthis from advancing further south towards the port of Aden, which is held by the internationally-recognized government.
The Houthis have frequently targeted Aden’s airport with missiles in recent weeks, after taking a stretch of Yemen’s Red Sea coast in September.
Hostilities between the Houthis, who are backed by Iran, and Saudi Arabia reignited in July, shattering a 2022 UN-brokered ceasefire that had largely halted fighting ⁠between the ‌two sides.
Ibrahim Dahman, Teele Rebane and Farida Elsebai contributed reporting.

articles.title_orig: Scoop: Lutnick stalled curbing Nvidia chip sales to China — again — after Oval Office showdown
articles.title_zh: Scoop: Lutnick stalled curbing Nvidia chip sales to China — again — after Oval Office showdown
articles.content_orig:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent challenged Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick over his department’s reluctance to label Nvidia customer Megaspeed a possible national security threat in a Situation Room confrontation last week that illustrates the tension inside the Trump administration over Chinese access to Nvidia’s advanced chips, two people familiar with the matter told CNN.
Trump officials have long harbored concerns that Megaspeed has circumvented US law and funneled advanced chips into China — a prospect that Treasury staffers argued should land it on Commerce’s so-called entity list of China-connected companies that could pose national security risks. But the issue gathered newfound attention and importance in recent days when Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang admitted to an affair with a Megaspeed employee suspected of being a Chinese spy.
Senior Trump officials, including Lutnick, also were briefed months ago about Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang, a Megaspeed executive who the intelligence community suspected of being a Chinese spy, people familiar with the matter said.
But despite those warnings, Commerce has so far refused to put Megaspeed on the entity list, the people said.
Confronted on it by Bessent last Thursday, Lutnick did not immediately commit to taking any specific action, they said.
Axios first reported the Situation Room confrontation.
Megaspeed is a Singapore-based company that was originally incorporated in 2015 as a Chinese video game developer called 7Road International. But in the three years since Alice Huang became director and the company changed its name, it has become one of the largest buyers of Nvidia chips in Asia , purchasing more than $4 billion worth of its semiconductors, by some analyst estimates.
Megaspeed has denied any wrongdoing and said it is a “compliant and legal company.” China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs called the allegations that Alice Huang was a Chinese spy “groundless speculation and an attempt to smear and malign China.”
The entity list represents one of the US’s most significant tools for preventing American firms from selling their products to foreign companies and organizations. But adding Megaspeed to the list could also risk inflaming tensions with China amid Trump’s efforts to manage the US’ trade relationship with the fellow superpower. The Commerce Department hasn’t added any company to the list in more than a year.
Representatives for the Treasury and Commerce departments did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

articles.title_orig: Spain: Housing crisis prompts first general strike in 14 years, before hundreds of thousands join protest
articles.title_zh: Spain: Housing crisis prompts first general strike in 14 years, before hundreds of thousands join protest
articles.content_orig:
Authorities in Spain say that despite pouring rain, some 120,000 citizens took to the streets of the capital, Madrid, on Wednesday evening after millions of striking workers brought Europe's fourth-largest economy to a standstill under the motto "Salaries. Housing. Prices" in the country's first general strike in 14 years earlier in the day.
The massive turnout came in response to housing shortages and unbearably high rents.
City officials in Barcelona said 55,000 people attended evening marches there as they walked behind a huge banner reading "Live. Not just survive." Housing activists in the city said the turnout was far larger, claiming that 400,000 had hit the streets.
As has been the case in other demonstrations across the Europea of late , peaceful protests later gave way to small groups of marauding young men who smashed storefront windows along Barcelona's main shopping street. They also set fire to dumpsters and shot fireworks at police when they arrived.
Earlier on Wednesday, workers across Spain gathered en masse, marching and setting up picket lines despite stormy weather in many areas of the country.
Symbolized by the eviction and death of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal in Madrid earlier this year, the crisis has also prompted a snap election set for November 29.
The government of left-wing Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez attempted to pass legislation to ease the plight of renters, but was blocked in parliament by opposition parties. Lacking the power to get legislation passed, Sanchez called the early vote in hopes of shoring up more support.
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
Sanchez's government did end up approving two extraordinary decrees introducing measures similar to the housing reforms rejected by parliament.
"We won't stop until we transform this country's housing model from top to bottom so that houses are for living instead of being at the service of the [landlord] minority," said Alicia del Rio, spokesperson for the Madrid Tenants' Union.
While most of the protests were peaceful, strikers in front of Madrid's Mercamadrid wholesale market said police had used pepper spray on the crowd, prompting at least 13 people to seek medical attention.
Some airlines later reported disruptions to flights in and out of Spain as some airport and airline workers participated in the strike.
The country has a deficit of about 750,000 homes, which is set ​to grow to more than a million by 2028, according to estimates from the central bank.
With fewer and fewer individuals and families able to buy a home, the number of renters in the country has risen sharply. According to Spain's youth council, the average rent is €1,176 ($1,315). This is equivalent to 99% of the average young person's salary.
The general strike came a day after rail workers launched a strike over two major deadly train crashes this year, making decrepit infrastructure another major issue in the upcoming parliamentary elections.
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
Spain's government supported Wednesday's strike, saying it was staged "in favor of rights" rather than against anyone. Sources close to Sanchez inner circle have gone so far as to say it is "against the opposition."
Alberto Nunez Feijoo, leader of the conservative People’s Party (PP), had a different take, saying if it was indeed "a strike against the opposition," it was "an absurdity the likes of which does not exist in any other European Union country."
Although the UGT labor union — one of the strike organizers — and Sanchez's socialist PSOE party are two separate institutions, they share a historic founder in Pablo Iglesias Posse.
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
Nicole Ris, reporting for DW in Madrid, followed the strike closely as it unfolded on Wednesday, saying earlier:
Here in Madrid, apparently, lots of people are still showing up for work, and people I know have clearly said they will not go on strike as they don't see much sense in it — although they all suffer under the cost of living crisis and the housing crisis.
There is also debate about this strike being an "election strike" that could benefit the current government.
"I'm not taking part in this. It's nonsense. The government is supporting it because they hope they'll get enough votes on the 29th so they can carry on," a doorman in Madrid told me.
The government supports the strike, claiming it is being held "in favor of rights" rather than against anyone. Sources close to Sanchez's inner circle have gone so far as to say it is "against the opposition," according to the media here.

CoreWeave ( CRWV ) stock surged as much as 25% on Wednesday after the neocloud infrastructure provider reported better-than-expected quarterly revenue and raised its revenue outlook, fueled by booming customer demand for AI compute capacity.
The company highlighted $9 billion in customer prepayments and deposits expected in the next three months, and said it does not plan to take on more expensive debt through 2027, easing concerns about how it will fund its expansion.
"Demand for compute is growing faster than the capacity to deliver that infrastructure and that is being echoed by the expansion of the margins that we are seeing on each additional contract," CoreWeave co-founder and CEO Michael Intrator said during the company's earnings call on Tuesday after the bell.
The company reported $3.66 billion in third quarter revenue versus consensus estimates of $3.56 billion, according to Bloomberg data. CoreWeave's loss per share of $1.27 came in narrower than the $1.46 expected by Wall Street. The company also raised its full-year revenue guidance to $13 billion to $13.3 billion, up from a prior target of $12 billion to $13 billion.
This price reflects trading activity during the overnight session on the Blue Ocean ATS, available 8 PM to 4 AM ET, Sunday through Thursday, when regular markets are closed.
CoreWeave stock has been battered in recent weeks, dropping more than 40% over the past month amid growing concerns about AI financing. A chart that went viral in October showed CoreWeave's spiking bond yields, underscoring concerns about the company's debt-heavy balance sheet and whether it can scale its business quickly enough to cover rising interest expenses.
Amid the sell-off, Nvidia ( NVDA ) CEO Jensen Huang tried to ease concerns about the company's debt-heavy balance sheet by stating he was "optimistic" and that its "cost of capital is actually decreasing."

articles.title_orig: Some under-25s should get less benefits, Milburn review to say
articles.title_zh: Some under-25s should get less benefits, Milburn review to say
articles.content_orig:
Some young people could see reductions to the benefits they are entitled to, under a radical overhaul of the system to be recommended by a government-commissioned review.
Alan Milburn's year-long report, which will be published on Tuesday, will recommend moving under-25s off the main sickness and disability benefits, the Times reported .
Milburn, a former Labour health secretary, has been tasked by the government with helping reduce the one in eight 18- to 24-year-olds in the UK who are not in education, employment or training - or "Neet".
He said on Wednesday night that his plans would not be "pain-free" and would affect both existing and new claimants.
His report is expected to recommend that under-25s are no longer able to claim the health element of universal credit or personal independence payment (Pip).
Instead, they would receive an allowance on the same basic rate as universal credit.
Some could be eligible for a new "additional cost allowance" to cover day-to-day costs related to their conditions.
But many claimants would receive less under the plans, which the government is set to take forward into legislation in the new year.
Milburn, a Labour MP from 1992 to 2010, is also expected to recommend an investment of billions into more employment support for young people, including work placements, job subsidies and one-to-one personal advisers.
Those with more severe disabilities and unable to work would get a new benefit paid at a higher rate.
Speaking to the Times about his report, Milburn said: "Candidly, it could mean that some people will get less financial support at the beginning of their benefit claim than under the current system.
"But actually, for young people, there's a different debate that we've got to resolve, which is whether the priority is their longer-term life chances or just their immediate shorter-term finances.
"I think what the current system does [is] it prioritises the latter over the former. I believe that's the wrong choice and it needs to be the other way around."
Just under one million young people in the UK are Neets , data from the Office for National Statistics (ONS) from April to June suggests. This was a rise of 3% on the same period last year.
Milburn's recommendations are likely to be backed by Prime Minister Andy Burnham but could prove controversial among Labour MPs, who opposed welfare reform under his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer.
The reforms would represent a radical overhaul of Britain's welfare system, at a time when there is heavy political pressure for the UK to find the money to spend more on defence.
If Milburn's recommendations were approved, it could take almost a decade for the British state to see monetary savings.
The new system "will need significant investment" and would involve "rebuilding the system from scratch," Milburn added.
He said that currently "you've got hundreds of thousands of young people stuck in a benefit system that is trapping them in poverty, giving them no prospect of prosperity or a job".
His new proposed system would involve an element of carrot and stick, where young people could lose some of their benefits if they did not engage with the extra work support options.
"A deal isn't a deal unless there are potential consequences," Milburn said. "Entitlements and responsibilities are two sides of the same coin."
A government spokesperson said: "We will always ensure there is a safety net for the most vulnerable and those who are unable to work.
"But the prime minister has been clear that we need a wholesale change in the way we support young people to grow up in this country, where we invest in their success rather than paying for failure."
