articles.title_orig: United Airlines Blocks A.I. Agents From Booking Flights on Customers’ Behalf
articles.title_zh: United Airlines Blocks A.I. Agents From Booking Flights on Customers’ Behalf
articles.content_orig:
United Airlines said on Wednesday that it is banning artificial intelligence agents from making flight reservations on behalf of travelers, citing security risks and the possibility that such actions could violate federal rules.
Many consumers are turning to AI agents such as Meta's Muse and OpenAI's dots to complete tasks ranging from researching products and tracking down deals to making purchases.
To make an airline booking, an AI agent requires access to a customer's personal information, including credentials like payment information. United has a problem with that, saying that "sharing account credentials with personal, third-party, AI assistants can expose sensitive information, and actions taken by these tools may result in unintended purchases, account changes, or use of MileagePlus miles."
The carrier also said that using an AI agent to, for example, check in for a flight could violate federal regulations, including rules requiring travelers to verify in person that their luggage does not contain banned substances.
"As a result, United is taking steps to restrict access — directly within our digital platforms and indirectly via travel agencies and aggregators — to prohibit use by unauthorized, third-party personal AI agents or assistants," said the airline, which is updating its booking and ticketing policies to reflect the new rule.
United's new policy suggests the company wants to retain control over the customer booking process, said Henry Harteveldt, an aviation analyst at Atmosphere Research Group.
"United is saying they don't want to add yet another, and potentially even more powerful, intermediary than they already face in terms of Google search, price-comparison metasearch sites and online travel agencies," he told CBS News. "Flight searches cost airlines money, and undoubtedly United wants to avoid the expense associated with the surge of AI bot flight searches."
Other airlines are taking a different tack to the emergence of AI agents. For example, Southwest has made its flight inventory viewable to ChatGPT users, who can access the airline's website through the AI app.
United fares will continue to be bookable through flight aggregators such as Kayak, Hopper and Google Flights, Harteveldt said, adding that "consumers shouldn't find it any more difficult to find good fares on the airline."
"But by blocking the AI bots, United won't make it any easier to find its fares, either," he said.
Kris  Van Cleave contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Active ScreenConnect attacks breach MSPs, impact dozens of organizations
articles.title_zh: Active ScreenConnect attacks breach MSPs, impact dozens of organizations
articles.content_orig:
Update 11/11/26: Added additional information from ConnectWise and Huntress.
ConnectWise is investigating an active malware campaign targeting managed service providers (MSPs) that uses compromised ScreenConnect environments to deploy rogue remote-access clients to customer devices.
As part of its investigation, ConnectWise has disabled five third-party ScreenConnect extensions across approximately 400 partner environments as a precaution, warning that they may be associated with the attacks.
The campaign was first discovered Wednesday by cybersecurity firm Huntress, which says it has identified six compromised MSPs and 286 affected endpoints across 47 organizations, and that the number of victims continues to rise.
"Our SOC is working an active campaign that started around 17:47 UTC today targeting cloud-hosted ScreenConnect instances," Huntress posted to Reddit .
"We are currently tracking 6 compromised MSPs and 286+ endpoints, and those numbers are climbing. ConnectWise is engaged and working this with us."
ScreenConnect is a remote access and support platform used by MSPs and IT teams to remotely manage and troubleshoot customer devices.
According to Huntress, attackers are using ScreenConnect's Run Command functionality to deploy rogue ScreenConnect clients on managed endpoints, providing remote access outside of the legitimate MSP's ScreenConnect environment.
The researchers also warned of a potentially more dangerous technique in which attackers can compromise an MSP technician's workstation when they initiate a ScreenConnect session with an infected customer device.
Spike Brandt, Principal Threat Intelligence Incident Commander at Huntress, told BleepingComputer that the activity appears to involve abusing legitimate functionality rather than exploiting a software vulnerability.
"This appears to be abuse of legitimate functionality, aided using custom-built tooling that is, in some cases, compiled on the fly on the victim’s computer," Brandt told BleepingComputer.
"We have no information about how a “patient zero” computer or machine would have initiated this attack."
Huntress said it began receiving alerts when rogue ScreenConnect clients appeared on monitored endpoints and subsequently retrieved attacker scripts that were still accessible to analyze how the attacks worked.
However, the precise mechanism allowing malware to spread from an infected endpoint to a technician's workstation has not been publicly explained.
In a security advisory published Wednesday night, ConnectWise confirmed unauthorized access to ScreenConnect partner accounts and the installation of unauthorized remote-access software in customer environments.
As part of its investigation, the company discovered five independent third-party extensions that may be associated with the attacks and disabled them across approximately 400 partner environments as a precaution.
ScreenConnect extensions are installed through its built-in Extensions marketplace via the ScreenConnect administration interface.
"Our initial assessment leads us to suspect the threat actor deployed additional remote-access software through independent 3rd party extensions that partners may have added to their environments," ConnectWise said.
The company stressed that having these extensions installed does not necessarily mean that a network was compromised and that the attacks remain under investigation.
"Disabling these 3rd party extensions is a precautionary containment measure. It does not establish that unauthorized software, persistence mechanisms, or access already present on affected devices has been removed," explained ConnectWise
While ConnectWise has disabled the extensions in affected cloud-hosted environments, it warned that on-premises ScreenConnect customers must disable them manually, as the company cannot do so from their end.
Partners were also instructed not to re-enable or reinstall the extensions until further guidance is available.
ConnectWise warned that disabling the extensions does not remove malicious software, persistence mechanisms, or unauthorized access that attackers may have already established on compromised endpoints.
The company advised partners to review authentication logs, extension installation records, administrative activity, Run Command history, and Toolbox records for suspicious activity.
It also urged technicians to avoid initiating interactive ScreenConnect sessions with potentially compromised devices and instead use separate security tools to investigate.
ConnectWise also said it has received reports of technician workstations being compromised during interactive ScreenConnect sessions, but these reports are still being confirmed.
The company added that it has no reason to believe partners that have not deployed the five identified extensions are impacted by this incident, but encouraged all partners to remain on heightened alert.
Huntress has not determined how the attackers are gaining access to affected MSP environments, but says its current telemetry points to compromised credentials or hijacked operator sessions.
Huntress also warned that sequential identifiers used by the attackers suggest additional MSPs may have been previously compromised.
"Sequential attacker-assigned tags suggest other MSPs may have been compromised earlier, so ScreenConnect users should check their Run Command history even if they haven’t received alerts," Huntress told BleepingComputer.
Huntress also shared indicators of compromise (IOCs) to help organizations identify malicious activity, including rogue ScreenConnect client IDs and infrastructure used by the attackers.

Rogue ScreenConnect client IDs: 2588ef5c15954b10 , ed630cc2c873b091
Installer pattern: /Bin/ScreenConnect.ClientSetup.msi?...&c=Exploited<N>
Files: Panel-Lateral.ps1 , runnew.cmd , ToolboxRelayUploader.exe , Run-Lateral-Full.bat
The researchers are urging MSPs to review their environments for signs of compromise and avoid initiating interactive ScreenConnect sessions with potentially infected endpoints.
Huntress also told BleepingComputer that its researchers have contacted ConnectWise, the VPS provider hosting the attacker's infrastructure, cloud providers whose dynamic DNS services were used in the attacks, and the broader MSP community.
BleepingComputer found an earlier malicious batch script that references one of the rogue ScreenConnect client IDs listed by Huntress, suggesting that the ID was used in malicious activity months before the current attacks were disclosed.
The script, named SSA-2026-STATEMENT-15518787.bat ( VirusTotal ), appears to impersonate a Social Security Administration statement and was first uploaded to VirusTotal on July 25, 2026.
The batch file attempts to add Microsoft Defender exclusions and creates persistence through the Windows Startup folder and the Run registry key.
It then contacts amexsafekeyupdate.com to retrieve installation commands for two separate installers.
VirusTotal sandbox activity associated with the sample includes downloads of ScreenConnect MSI installers from cdn007-digitaldownloads[.]com and cyberrexdesign.screenconnect[.]com , with cdn007-digitaldownloads[.]com also listed by Huntress as a possible C2 domain.
After launching the second installer, the script uses PowerShell to search running processes and Windows services for ed630cc2c873b091 , one of the rogue ScreenConnect client IDs identified by Huntress.
If the identifier is found, the script considers the installation successful and sends a notification to the attackers through Telegram.
The earlier script also appears designed for a different distribution campaign, with its Social Security-themed filename suggesting it

articles.title_orig: Iran escalates in Hormuz, claims strike on Omani island it says 'enemy' uses for US military ops
articles.title_zh: Iran escalates in Hormuz, claims strike on Omani island it says 'enemy' uses for US military ops
articles.content_orig:
The IRGC reported a strike against ‘enemy navigation aid systems,’ radar and communications equipment located on Didamar Island in Hormuz (Credit: Reuters).
Iran claims it struck a small Omani island in the Strait of Hormuz , targeting oil tanker navigation infrastructure as CENTCOM maintains its blockade of Iranian ports and protects commercial shipping from Iranian attacks along the southern route.
Three sources also confirmed to Reuters Wednesday that navigation systems and communications equipment on Didamar Island, also known as Little Quoin Island, had been attacked, raising concerns about the vulnerability of maritime infrastructure used to maintain oil shipments through the Gulf.
Iran's semiofficial Fars News Agency reported that the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) navy targeted the island, alleging the systems were being used to help vessels transit the strait without Tehran's authorization.
WHITE HOUSE SILENT ON IRAN-OMAN HORMUZ PLAN TEHRAN SAYS WOULD BAN US WARSHIPS
A satellite image shows Didamar Island, Oman (Google/Airbus/Handout via Reuters)
Iranian state television also claimed that personnel and equipment on the island "were helping the flow of oil smuggling by the enemy," with the IRGC maintaining it had carried out the strikes, Reuters reported.
Video published by Reuters showed smoke rising near the rocky outcrop.
The Institute for the Study of War (ISW) said it identified the attack as occurring Nov. 8, before Iranian state media claimed responsibility on Nov. 10.
ISW also questioned the extent of the reported damage, noting that commercial vessels continued using the southern route after the attack.
"The extent of the damage to these systems and the systems struck remains unclear at the time of this writing," ISW said in its assessment.
Satellite imagery from the European Union's Copernicus Sentinel-2 program, cited by Reuters and dated Nov. 8, also showed apparent scorch marks near radar and radio equipment on the island.
TRADE VESSEL STRUCK BY PROJECTILE IN STRAIT OF HORMUZ AMID US-IRAN TALKS
A ship passes through the Strait of Hormuz during a two-week temporary ceasefire between the United States and Iran April 8, 2026. (Shady Alassar/Anadolu/Getty Images)
The strike comes as U.S. forces carry out missions to escort ships through the Strait of Hormuz, which connects the Persian Gulf to the Gulf of Oman and the Arabian Sea.
The U.S. Navy imposed its blockade of Iranian ports in April after Iran closed the Strait of Hormuz in February amid escalating tensions. The U.S. lifted the blockade in June following a temporary ceasefire agreement, but then reinstated it in July.
Commercial and allied shipping through the waterway is advised to use a southern route through Omani territorial waters, located outside of Tehran’s direct military control and overseen by CENTCOM.
The latest incident on Didamar Island comes as Gulf oil exporters work to restore shipments disrupted by the conflict.
TRUMP MEETS KEY IRAN WAR MEDIATOR AS UAE REVEALS MAJOR OIL EXPORT SURGE DESPITE CONFLICT
An Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps speedboat sails in the Persian Gulf during an IRGC marine parade marking Persian Gulf National Day near the Bushehr nuclear power plant in Bushehr, Iran, April 29, 2024. (Morteza Nikoubazl/NurPhoto via Getty Images)
According to Reuters, regional oil exports recovered to more than 80% of prewar levels in September and October, aided by CENTCOM and increased Saudi exports through the Red Sea.
Shipping companies have also relied on offshore tanker-to-tanker transfers near Oman and the United Arab Emirates to maintain flows.
Didamar, meanwhile, belongs to Oman, making the reported attack particularly sensitive as Tehran seeks to disrupt maritime operations in the region. It is a small, uninhabited rocky island roughly 10 nautical miles north of the tip of Oman's Musandam Peninsula, near one of the principal commercial shipping routes through the strait.
The island has long served as a navigational landmark for vessels traveling along the waterway, including through a lighthouse established in 1914.
Its maritime infrastructure reportedly includes a radar system mounted on a roughly 25-meter tower and radio communications equipment used to assist vessels navigating the narrow passage.
The island has also been associated with the Hormuz Control Centre, which coordinates maritime traffic in the area.
OIL SQUEEZE TIGHTENS AS IRAN-BACKED ATTACKS CRIPPLE HORMUZ ESCAPE ROUTES
A satellite image shows the Strait of Hormuz, a key maritime passage connecting the Persian Gulf to the Gulf of Oman, vital for global energy supply. (Amanda Macias/Fox News Digital)
Arabian Maritime and Navigation Aids Services (AMMAS) has been identified as a provider of navigational support infrastructure in the region, including maritime lights, buoys and other equipment.
The reported Didamar attack also follows U.S. military operations against Iranian targets elsewhere in the waterway.
U.S. forces struck targets on Iran's Qeshm Island Nov. 2, and officials described the strikes as "defensive" actions targeting Iranian surface-to-air missile threats.
Qeshm Island, located near the Strait of Hormuz, is home to Iranian naval facilities and military infrastructure associated with the Revolutionary Guard.
President Donald Trump also acknowledged Nov. 6 that American forces continue to conduct limited strikes against Iranian targets.

Asked by a reporter about the strikes near Qeshm Island, Trump said, "I don't want to talk about it. We do minor strikes. They built a little bit of an anti-aircraft device, and we knocked it out in about 15 minutes, maybe five."

articles.title_orig: Lego marketplace BrickLink offline after 'unusual activity' detected
articles.title_zh: Lego marketplace BrickLink offline after 'unusual activity' detected
articles.content_orig:
Lego has taken its online marketplace BrickLink offline after detecting what it described as unusual activity on the platform.
BrickLink is used by Lego collectors worldwide to buy and sell secondhand Lego sets, source new bricks and purchase limited edition releases.
It was originally set up by a fan, but Lego acquired it in 2019. In a homepage message, the firm said that before restoring BrickLink, it wanted to "fully understand" what had happened.
"That means containing the issue, investigating how it happened and checking for related issues," Lego said. It did not provide any further detail about whether the site has been breached or hacked, and whether any customer data was affected.
After being contacted by the BBC, Lego published the update.
BrickLink has been offline for the last three days, with a previous message saying it was down for maintenance.
Cyber-professional Melanie Hoskin has been collecting Lego for 45 years and is a regular user of BrickLink.
She told the BBC she had received multiple links for payment for a limited edition release she had pre-ordered on the platform, after she had already paid for it.
She said Lego did not believe that the payment had been taken and at one point said it would ban her from BrickLink.
The problem has now been resolved and Lego said it was not aware of wider payment issues.
It is unclear if the payment glitch had any connection to the issue that led to the website going offline.
Hoskin said she felt like she had been accused of theft.
"Lego is my stress relief," she said. "Lego is what I grew up with as a kid, it's what bonded me with my sisters.
"I've got a Lego room and I've not even been able to walk into it this past couple of weeks because it just angers me."
Earlier today, a message on BrickLink said the platform would be back online by Wednesday evening, but that message has now been deleted and there is no longer a time frame given for its return.

articles.title_orig: Michel Houellebecq, French Writer, Is Investigated Over Anti-Muslim Remarks
articles.title_zh: Michel Houellebecq, French Writer, Is Investigated Over Anti-Muslim Remarks
articles.content_orig:
French novelist Michel Houellebecq has been charged in a court in Paris, France, for ‘complicity in incitement to discrimination, hatred or violence against a group of people on account of their origin or their belonging or not belonging to a particular ethnicity, nation, race or religion’. The news was originally broken by the French news site Le Figaro on Tuesday, 10 November.
Houellebecq gave an interview to the right-wing magazine Front Populaire in November 2022. In it, he made several controversial statements about Muslim immigration.
For example, he told the magazine, ‘The wish of the population with French roots, as the phrase goes, is not for Muslims to assimilate, but for them to stop stealing from and assaulting them, in short, for the violence to decrease, for them to respect the law and people. Or, another good solution, for them to leave.’
The writer also stated that he is surprised that the ‘great replacement theory’—the idea that elites are importing immigrants to Europe to replace the native European population on purpose—is called a ‘theory’, since he believes ‘it’s not a theory, it’s a fact’. The most prominent proponent of the great replacement theory is another French author, Renaud Camus .
However, the statements that most likely caused the most trouble for Houellebecq were the ones he made about violence against Muslim immigrants. He said in the interview with Front Populaire that, ‘When entire territories come under Islamist control, I think acts of resistance will take place…There will be attacks and shootings in mosques, in cafés frequented by Muslims, in short, Bataclan in reverse.’
Here, he is referencing the attack on the Bataclan theatre in Paris in November 2015 by radical Islamist terrorists.
The Movement against Racism and for Friendship Between Peoples (MRAP) and the Union of Mosques of France are the ‘civil parties’ aiding the French state in the prosecution of Houellebecq.
Free speech rights are protected in the preamble to the current Constitution of the Fifth Republic of France, giving full constitutional force to the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen of 1789. However, despite this, the French criminal code includes strong hate speech laws.
Houellebecq’s two attorneys have released a joint statement, declaring that ‘The incriminated remarks have no dimension of incitement, not even implicitly, and therefore fall within the bounds of freedom of opinion and expression’ and that their client’s ‘place is not in a courtroom’.

articles.title_orig: Lutnick stalled Trump crackdown on diversion of Nvidia chips to China, Axios reports
articles.title_zh: Lutnick stalled Trump crackdown on diversion of Nvidia chips to China, Axios reports
articles.content_orig:
Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged in Please refresh your browser to be logged in
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
Cloud computing firm Megaspeed has come under fresh scrutiny as the US looks into Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with a businesswoman alleged to be a Chinese spy .
Nvidia has seen hundreds of billions of dollars wiped from its value in recent days after the US chipmaker said it would investigate Huang’s admitted relationship with the former Megaspeed director Alice Huang .
China says allegations about Chinese spies are “entirely groundless” and “intended to smear and malign China”. But US intelligence officials nevertheless believe Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, was funneling information to Beijing .
For years, Washington has tried to keep China from gaining the know-how to rival the United States in cutting-edge AI, which Nvidia’s chips support.
Now attention turns to Megaspeed over suspicions that it helped Beijing ‌gain access ⁠to advanced AI chips whose export to China is restricted.
Megaspeed was incorporated in 2015 as 7Road International before changing its name to Megaspeed International in March 2023, when it was bought by a British Virgin Islands company called Huang Le Ltd.
Alice Huang ended her eight month tenure as managing director months later, in October 2023, but is reported to still be involved in the company. In November 2023, the firm was sold again to a Singaporean entity called Swiftdata, which says its main job is providing hosting services by non-data centres.
Megaspeed's assets increased sharply to $3 billion in 2024 from $33 million in 2023, its business filings showed.
The company soon became one of Nvidia’s biggest Asian customers and grew rapidly as a link between the US chipmaker and the Chinese tech group Alibaba. Two Singapore citizens are listed as officers of both Megaspeed and Swiftdata.
Singapore has come under mounting pressure from the US to clamp down on companies suspected of transferring advanced AI chips to Chinese firms. But the city-state does not necessarily exclude such transfers.
Singaporean police are now conducting their own investigation into Megaspeed, in step with US authorities. US intelligence officials have already concluded Alice Huang was a Chinese intelligence asset, according to the New York Times .
US intelligence officials have reportedly been alert to Alice Huang’s position for some time. According to the New York Times , US president Donald Trump was briefed on intelligence findings around a year ago but chose to do nothing with them.
It was late last year that US authorities began investigating Megaspeed over suspicions it was helping to divert Nvidia chips to China.
Singapore police said they would investigate the firm over “suspected breaches of our domestic laws” after a US senator asked the commerce department to look into related concerns.
According to the NYT, officials suspected it was Alice Huang who was feeding information directly to Beijing on how to gain access to the advanced AI chips.
Megaspeed has denied any wrongdoing and told the newspaper that it was “committed to getting to the facts behind these allegations” and would welcome a “formal, evidence-based investigation”.
It said in a statement last year that “there has been no evidence of any violations concerning the illicit transfer of chips or any illegal activities”.
And Nvidia said Megaspeed was just like any other regional customer, and that such customers only “receive ordinary business information - not sensitive Nvidia trade secrets - and zero information relevant to national security”.
For all the concerns above, the affair between Alice Huang and Nvidia’s Jensen Huang has rocked the tech and political worlds. It remains unclear how long the affair lasted, and when exactly the relationship might have ended.
Alice Huang was a Chinese finance executive before becoming involved in artificial intelligence, data centers and computer chips. She became Megaspeed’s controlling shareholder in March 2023, according to research by the C4ADS, a Washington-based nonprofit focused on global security.
But by November 2023, she was no longer listed as a director, and all her shares were transferred to a Singaporean businessman, Tan Yong Pong, who also is known as James Tan.
While public records suggest Alice Huang left Megaspeed, short seller Culper Research issued a report in May this year that cited a Megaspeed employee saying Huang was “actually still our boss” and was still involved in the company’s daily operations.
Before Megaspeed, Alice Huang previously held senior positions at the Chinese firm Shanghai Hexi Investment Co. from around 2015 to 2017, according to social media posts and records from Simuwang, a Chinese private equity database.
Before that, she worked at HSBC’s Hong Kong private banking arm and at CITIC Securities, a Chinese investment bank.

articles.title_orig: Hands on with Home Assistant’s new ‘smart home multi-tool’
articles.title_zh: Hands on with Home Assistant’s new ‘smart home multi-tool’
articles.content_orig:
The Home Assistant Connect Aux-2 helped me track my fridge temperature and finally set up my in-wall speakers.﻿
If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.
If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.
Nabu Casa — the commercial side of the Open Home Foundation , which runs Home Assistant — just launched the Home Assistant Connect Aux-2 , a multi-function box designed to help you bring more non-smart devices into your smart home. It’s part of Home Assistant’s ongoing efforts to become more user-friendly . And it’s working.
I’ve been testing the Aux-2 for a couple days and I’ve found it unsurprisingly useful and surprisingly easy to set up. The Aux-2 is a $69 box about the size of a deck of cards. It has 2.4GHz Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, Ethernet, USB-A, USB-C, a digital/analog audio jack, a Grove port for interfacing with peripherals like sensors, buttons, and LEDs , and a pair of RS-232 serial ports.
It can bridge Bluetooth devices into your Home Assistant setup. Its USB port lets you plug in a Nabu Casa Z-Wave or Zigbee antenna in case your Home Assistant hub isn’t in a good spot. You can control devices like TVs, AV receivers, solar inverters, and more via serial connector. And you can connect an amplifier or powered speakers to its audio jack to stream music to older audio equipment.
All of these things leverage Home Assistant’s capabilities as an open-source platform. The Aux-2 is based on ESPHome , an open platform for making DIY smart home devices from cheap, flexible ESP boards, and it uses existing Home Assistant/ESPHome integrations for all its features. The serial integration was developed earlier this year ; Music Assistant and SendSpin , which power the audio-out feature, are in active development.
I have a Home Assistant install, but even after several years it is not my primary smart home platform simply because of friction and time constraints. Instead, I have a hodgepodge of Google Home, Apple Home, and a few devices that are only in Home Assistant. The situation is not ideal.
But the Aux-2’s capabilities perfectly intersect with two things I’d been meaning to do anyway, one of which I’m already using Home Assistant for. First, I have a garage fridge, because I live in Texas. I also have children, which means sometimes the fridge or freezer door gets left open. I want to know when that happens before all my food goes bad.
A couple years ago, I set up a few Aqara temperature sensors, connected to Home Assistant via a now-discontinued Zigbee dongle , and set up an automation to alert me if the fridge or freezer get too warm. But they frequently drop connection (probably because they’re inside a fridge in the garage), they chew through coin cell batteries, and they have no displays, which means I also have a cheap Acu-rite hygrometer in the fridge so I can see the temperature without pulling out my phone. Someone tipped me off to Govee’s Bluetooth hygrometers , but I’d need a Bluetooth proxy to get them into Home Assistant. That happens to be a feature of the Aux-2.
I also have a set of in-wall speakers in my living room that I’ve never used. I’d been meaning to get an amp, but analysis paralysis set in. Do I get a Wiim Amp? A stereo receiver? A cheap Bluetooth amp? Do I try to get them to work with my four Sonos speakers? Maybe my ancient Google Home speaker? Turns out I do nothing for five years. Maybe the Aux-2 could help.
Setting up the Aux-2 was much easier than I expected. I plugged it into my computer via USB-C and was able to download and install the latest firmware right from a browser. I could also add my Wi-Fi credentials. Then I unplugged it, moved it over to my media console and connected it to power (it takes USB-C or power over Ethernet), and did the rest of the setup in the Home Assistant interface.
In HA, I was prompted to install ESPHome, which discovered the Aux-2 and sent me to a “set up your ESPHome device page” that walked me through the capabilities. Enabling Bluetooth proxying took a couple of clicks; I added the Govee Bluetooth integration and put batteries into the sensors and they showed up automatically. Mercifully, they maintained their Bluetooth connection through three walls and a fridge, and now my fridge monitoring setup works again.
The audio capability took a little longer, but most of that was spent hooking the speakers up to the amp I ended up buying and setting up Music Assistant , which I didn’t have installed. Music Assistant lives on your Home Assistant hardware and can play from many different services — from Spotify to YouTube Music to local files and more — and to many different outputs, like Sonos, Wiim, AirPlay, Google Cast, and others, but they all need to be configured, and that took a beat. Not a long beat: less than half an hour total.
I can now play music to the in-wall speakers using Music Assistant. Sendspin , the whole-home audio standard (also developed by the Open Home Foundation) is supposed to be able to let you group speakers from different protocols under certain conditions, but I haven’t gotten that working yet. The standard is still in development, and I’ve also been busy, so I’m not sure if that’s a me problem or a them problem.
I would also like to see the Aux-2 show up as an AirPlay or Spotify Connect target, which (again) is probably just a thing I need to set up.
Serial control is the most intriguing feature of the Aux-2, and it’s unfortunately the thing I haven’t yet had time to test. But the ability to hook in things like solar inverters, TVs, and receivers is fascinating and one I want to look into further when I get the chance. Maybe I’ll hook it up to my LG TV.
The Aux-2 doesn’t do anything you couldn’t do already with an ESP32 board and various accessories, or even other ESP-based devices. The Apollo Automations Cast-1 , for example, costs $35 and supports the same music-casting and Bluetooth proxy features I’m actually using from the Aux-2 at the moment. You could bodge together something even cheaper with DIY parts.
That’s not a knock against the Aux-2. That’s the whole point . The ecosystem is open by design, which I find endlessly refreshing. Both Nabu Casa and Apollo fund the Open Home Foundation, which develops Home Assistant and ESPHome (and Sendspin and Music Assistant), and both provide hardware that’s a little easier to use than DIY options. But there’s nothing stopping you from making your own devices. It’s actively encouraged.
I bought a three-pack of ESP32 boards for $16 three years ago. I could have built a Bluetooth proxy from one of those. I could have built an LED controller. I could have built a soil sensor, or a media player, or any of a dozen other things. I didn’t do anything at all.
But now that I’ve used the Aux-2 and dipped my toe into the ESPHome waters, maybe I will.

articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
CoreWeave ( CRWV ) stock surged as much as 25% on Wednesday after the neocloud infrastructure provider reported better-than-expected quarterly revenue and raised its revenue outlook, fueled by booming customer demand for AI compute capacity.
The company highlighted $9 billion in customer prepayments and deposits expected in the next three months, and said it does not plan to take on more expensive debt through 2027, easing concerns about how it will fund its expansion.
"Demand for compute is growing faster than the capacity to deliver that infrastructure and that is being echoed by the expansion of the margins that we are seeing on each additional contract," CoreWeave co-founder and CEO Michael Intrator said during the company's earnings call on Tuesday after the bell.
The company reported $3.66 billion in third quarter revenue versus consensus estimates of $3.56 billion, according to Bloomberg data. CoreWeave's loss per share of $1.27 came in narrower than the $1.46 expected by Wall Street. The company also raised its full-year revenue guidance to $13 billion to $13.3 billion, up from a prior target of $12 billion to $13 billion.
This price reflects trading activity during the overnight session on the Blue Ocean ATS, available 8 PM to 4 AM ET, Sunday through Thursday, when regular markets are closed.
CoreWeave stock has been battered in recent weeks, dropping more than 40% over the past month amid growing concerns about AI financing. A chart that went viral in October showed CoreWeave's spiking bond yields, underscoring concerns about the company's debt-heavy balance sheet and whether it can scale its business quickly enough to cover rising interest expenses.
Amid the sell-off, Nvidia ( NVDA ) CEO Jensen Huang tried to ease concerns about the company's debt-heavy balance sheet by stating he was "optimistic" and that its "cost of capital is actually decreasing."
Ines Ferre is a senior business reporter for Yahoo Finance.

articles.title_orig: Why Nvidia Stock Rose Today Despite Calls for CEO Jensen Huang to Step Down
articles.title_zh: Why Nvidia Stock Rose Today Despite Calls for CEO Jensen Huang to Step Down
articles.content_orig:
Shares of Nvidia fell more than 7% in after-hours trading on Wednesday after The Wall Street Journal reported that the company's board is preparing to oust CEO Jensen Huang .
The news landed minutes after The New York Times reported that Huang had an extramarital relationship with another executive at the company.
The alleged relationship was with Kimberly Powell, vice president of health care at Nvidia, according to the report. Powell's bio on the Nvidia website says she's "responsible for the company's worldwide healthcare business, including hardware and software platforms for accelerated computing, AI, and visualization that power the ecosystem of medical imaging, life sciences, drug discovery, and healthcare analytics."
Huang and Powell were reportedly captured on camera being affectionate with one another at a hotel in San Jose, California in March, according to the Times.
Nvidia did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment. Heller, the crisis PR firm Huang reportedly hired as early as last year, did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment.
The report comes days after Huang admitted to an affair with a woman who is believed by U.S. intelligence of being a Chinese spy. The CEO was romantically involved with Alice Huang, according to The Financial Times , who U.S. intelligence officials believe is a spy for China's Ministry of State Security, The New York Times reported.
Nvidia's board of directors has opened an independent investigation and hired the law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to look into the spying allegations.
"I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did," Huang wrote in the message to Nvidia staff on Sunday. "I am deeply sorry."
Rumors of an affair between Huang and Powell have circulated for years, in part because Powell lacks a background in health or science, according to a former employee who asked not to be named because of the sensitivity of the matter.
Nvidia's stock is down 7% this week and is on pace for its sixth straight weekly slide, reflecting broad concern on the sustainability of the artificial intelligence buildout. The AI infrastructure trade was hit particularly hard last week after the midterm elections, as Democrats won sweeping majorities in both houses of Congress, and dozens of ballot measures past that could make building data centers more difficult.

articles.title_orig: Feds arrest top official of healthcare company, alleging illegal drug importation
articles.title_zh: Feds arrest top official of healthcare company, alleging illegal drug importation
articles.content_orig:
U.S. authorities are accusing the two top officials of a Canadian company of operating a long-running scheme to illegally import prescription drugs into the U.S., according to court records filed Tuesday.
John Thomas Howard, treasurer and a director of the company, CANARX, was arrested Sunday on smuggling and conspiracy charges, according to the records.
Bob Howard, his brother, who is president and a director of CANARX, is also wanted in the federal investigation, according to an affidavit from Dustin Dobbs, a special agent with the Food and Drug Administration's Office of Criminal Investigations. He has not yet been taken into custody.
Besides conspiracy and smuggling, the arrest warrant said John Thomas Howard was charged with introducing misbranded drugs into interstate commerce and illegal drug importation. No plea has been filed.
CANARX was featured in a CNBC investigation last year that revealed how the company and others known as alternative funding programs, or AFPs, are becoming more pervasive around the U.S. as drug costs skyrocket. The investigation found these companies have penetrated the country's healthcare system by offering high-cost specialty drugs at more affordable prices through private and public employers. In some cases, employers are requiring their staff to use an AFP.
AFPs often obtain the medications overseas and ship them directly to patients, a practice that federal authorities have said is illegal and poses safety risks. CNBC traced the trail of drugs from abroad to the U.S. via a supply chain that the pharmaceutical companies producing the medications have not authorized.
On its website, CANARX, founded in 2002 and based in Windsor, Ontario, Canada, described its business as the first international prescription provider for the U.S. and the safest such program in the industry. The company said it sources its medications from Canada, the United Kingdom, Australia and New Zealand.
But the affidavit said that the FDA's investigation found "there is probable cause to believe that (CANARX) illegally imported or caused the illegal importation of prescription drugs into the United States …."
The affidavit does not specify which medications the agency believes were illegally imported. The criminal complaint covers the period from Feb. 22, 2017, through April 15, 2026.
The company's general counsel, Joseph Morris, told CNBC in a statement: "The Howards deny all the charges against them, will defend vigorously, and expect to be vindicated in court."
The company has been under FDA scrutiny for several years. In 2023, the agency seized medication being shipped by CANARX that it says was potentially misbranded and counterfeit, according to an email sent to a patient that was obtained by CNBC.
And in 2019, the FDA sent a warning letter to the company, saying it was operating "in a manner that substitutes the FDA-approved drugs prescribed by the U.S. healthcare provider with unapproved drugs." Morris, in response to that warning, argued CANARX was not misleading patients, but agreed for the company to stop importing drugs that need to be administered by a doctor.
In an interview as part of the CNBC investigation, Morris said last year that the medicines shipped to U.S. patients come from highly regulated countries. He said CANARX was operating legally.
The central question for AFPs is the legality of importing prescription drugs into the U.S. for personal use. The FDA allows Americans to import medications for individual use in some cases if the drug is not available domestically. That is the basis on which the AFPs built their models for shipping medicines directly to patients.
But an FDA spokesperson told CNBC last year that "in most circumstances, a person cannot import prescription drugs from other countries into the U.S. ... as substitutes for FDA-approved drugs."
In a separate civil lawsuit that is pending, Gilead Sciences accused CANARX and other companies of illegally importing Biktarvy, its medication to treat HIV.
In a statement to CNBC on Wednesday, a Gilead spokesperson said the company "has taken strong legal action to protect patients and the integrity of the U.S. medicines supply chain. We welcome the government's efforts to hold accountable those whose conduct may put patients at risk."
CANARX has not responded to the Gilead lawsuit.
— CNBC's Paige Tortorelli and Melissa Lee contributed to this report

articles.content_orig:

By Chuck Mikolajczak and Utkarsh Hathi
NEW YORK, Nov 11 (Reuters) - US stocks closed higher on Wednesday, with the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq each rallying more than 1% as earnings from neocloud firm CoreWeave cooled investor concerns about the durability of the AI trade, while Nvidia stabilized after two straight ‌sessions of sharp declines.
Battered CoreWeave shares surged 24.7%, their biggest daily percentage jump in more than three months, to close at the highest level in two ‌weeks. The company said it would become profitable in the first half of 2028 on an adjusted basis, seeking to reassure investors that strong demand and customer commitments could support its debt-fueled expansion.
Sentiment improved across ​AI infrastructure stocks, as Nebius Group surged 15.4% and Applied Digital shot up 7.4%.
Nvidia advanced after shedding about $430 billion of market capitalization in the previous two sessions as investors worried about CEO Jensen Huang's relationship with a businesswoman alleged to be a Chinese spy.
Equities have been volatile in recent days. Investors have expressed concerns about more regulation in the AI space after sweeping Democratic victories in the US midterm elections last week. That, and worries about Nvidia's leadership, pressured one of the biggest pillars of the current bull market.
Contributing to choppy stock ‌trading, investors have been encouraged by cooling oil prices but ⁠concerned by hot inflation data that pushed Treasury yields sharply higher.
"Everybody's looking for a canary in a coal mine every single day, every minute of every day, and then they're reacting every single day," said Thomas Martin, senior portfolio manager at Globalt in Atlanta.
"What ⁠we've seen is that you've gone back and forth, back and forth, back and forth between AI is good, AI is not so good. We're worried about it, then oh, it's great."
The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 254.60 points, or 0.49%, to 52,486.49, the S&P 500 gained 98.45 points, or 1.31%, to 7,619.38 and the Nasdaq Composite gained 400.31 points, or 1.60%, to 25,466.19.
TECH SECTOR LEADS ​MARKET ​GAINS
The Philadelphia SE Semiconductor index jumped 5.7% to close at its highest since November 3. Every component of the index advanced.
Recent pronounced selling ​pressure prompted some investors to buy the dip, but early indicators show ‌it is too soon to sound the all-clear.
Investors bought equities even during last week's selloff, with all net inflows coming through ETFs and institutional clients leading the purchases, Bank of America Global Research analysts said in a note.
The S&P 500 technology index, up 2.7%, was the best-performing of the 11 major S&P sectors and has risen in three of the past four sessions.
The CBOE Volatility Index fell for the fourth straight session to close at a one-week low of 17.49. Last week, Wall Street's fear gauge hit its highest in more than seven months.
ANTHROPIC IPO DRAWS ATTENTION
Investors also examined the terms set by Anthropic on Tuesday for its blockbuster initial public offering. The Claude chatbot creator ‌is aiming for a valuation of up to $1.4 trillion in the share sale.
Vanda Research said in ​a note that the IPO could attract record buying by retail investors, with the potential to surpass ​SpaceX as one of the biggest single-day retail purchases ever.
Hotter-than-expected inflation data on ​Tuesday cemented market expectations the US Federal Reserve would raise interest rates next month, with traders now fully pricing in a hike ‌of at least 25 basis points and a 10.4% chance of ​an increase of 50 basis points, according ​to CME FedWatch.
Comments from multiple Fed officials also suggested the US central bank was open to a more aggressive path of rate hikes as price pressures worsen.
The US bond market was shut on Wednesday for Veterans Day.
Advancing issues outnumbered decliners by a 1.48-to-1 ratio on the NYSE and by a 1.77-to-1 ratio on ​the Nasdaq.
The S&P 500 posted 17 new 52-week highs and ‌no new lows, while the Nasdaq Composite recorded 77 new highs and 159 new lows.
Volume on US exchanges was 14.74 billion shares, compared with ​the 18.68 billion average for the full session over the last 20 trading days.

articles.title_orig: US auto workers union urges Congress to keep its eye on Chinese automakers
articles.title_zh: US auto workers union urges Congress to keep its eye on Chinese automakers
articles.content_orig:
WASHINGTON, Nov 11 (Reuters) – The United Auto Workers union urged top US lawmakers to keep the House China Select Committee in place when Democrats take over, citing concerns about ​Chinese automakers, according to a letter seen by Reuters on ‌Wednesday.
“From global overcapacity in electric vehicles, Chinese ownership of Western automakers, and continued offshoring to China, we urgently need Congress’s focused attention on these issues and their rapidly emerging downstream effects,” the UAW wrote House Speaker Mike Johnson and Democratic Leader ‌Hakeem ​Jeffries. “Autoworkers cannot afford any lapse in Congress’s ⁠attention on this issue.”
Jeffries said ⁠this week he would meet with Democratic leaders on the future of the House China select committee.
The House select committee under Republican Representative John Moolenaar has investigated a number of China-related issues, including ​Ford’s partnership with Chinese battery company CATL and an abandoned plan of a subsidiary of Chinese battery company Gotion to build a $2.4 ⁠billion plant in Michigan to produce battery ⁠materials.
Moolenaar said this week the committee work should continue ​next year. “The challenges we face as a nation are only becoming more ​urgent given the high-stakes technology competition in AI and (China’s) growing coercion ‌targeting America’s allies and partners,” he said.
Congress has yet to pass legislation to make permanent a ban on Chinese autos. Senator Bernie Moreno, a Republican co-author of the bill, told Reuters on Tuesday he was ⁠getting “really, really close” to a deal and hoping for a Senate vote as early as next week.
“Congress must ensure that China and its practices do ⁠not gain a foothold ‌in the US market,” the UAW letter said.
A ⁠group representing General Motors, Toyota, Volkswagen and other major ​automakers ‌is lobbying Congress to complete work on the Chinese ​auto ban ⁠this year.
A regulation imposed by former President Joe Biden in early 2025 effectively banned Chinese automakers from selling or building passenger vehicles in the US because they could send sensitive driver data to China. Washington also maintains more than 100% tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles.
(Reporting by David Shepardson; Editing ​by David Gregorio)

Stocks were higher Wednesday, boosted by sharp gains in CoreWeave and a rebound in Nvidia following back-to-back losing sessions for the chipmaker.
The Nasdaq Composite jumped 1.60% to end at 25,466.19, while the S&P 500 advanced 1.31% to 7,619.38. The Dow Jones Industrial Average gained 254.60 points, or 0.49%, and closed at 52,486.49.
Neocloud stock CoreWeave rallied nearly 25% after reporting third-quarter revenue that beat analyst expectations. CoreWeave also lifted operating income and revenue guidance for 2026.
Nvidia, meanwhile, climbed 2.9% after dropping nearly 10% to start the week when CEO Jensen Huang confirmed he had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy. The pullback in Nvidia weighed on the broader market Tuesday, with the major averages ending the session lower.
Artificial intelligence lab Anthropic on Tuesday said in an updated Securities and Exchange Commission filing that it will offer 825 million shares in an initial public offering planned for next week that could value the five-year-old company at as much as $1.4 trillion.
"The sentiment bump coming from CoreWeave results and Anthropic IPO demand is helping the broader ecosystem," Ross Mayfield, an investment strategist at Baird Private Wealth Management, told CNBC. "Markets are continuing to unwind last week's overshoot to the downside with cleaner positioning now a tailwind and an attractive near-term valuation/earnings story in a lot of the AI stocks."
Equities fell on Tuesday after stronger-than-expected October inflation data renewed expectations that the Federal Reserve will again raise interest rates at its final policy meeting of the year in December. The consumer price index increased by 0.4% month over month in October , topping economists' estimates.
Chicago Federal Reserve President Austan Goolsbee sounded the alarm over that latest CPI figure.
"It's another distressing report — borderline disturbing," Goolsbee said Tuesday in an interview with "PBS NewsHour ."
Expectations for a quarter-point rate increase next month rose to about 90% following the Dept. of Labor release, according to the CME Group's FedWatch tool.
"Despite some technical uncertainty, higher than desired levels of inflation should keep the Fed in a stance of dissatisfaction with the degree of progress on inflation remaining lackluster, so hiking the Fed Funds policy rate in December is our and the market's base case," wrote Rick Rieder, CIO of global fixed income at BlackRock. "The question now is more of one of the extent of the hike."
Comments from Fed Governor Christopher Waller at a Bank of England conference in London Tuesday also led traders to price in a greater chance of a quarter-point move.
The U.S. bond market was closed on Wednesday for Veterans Day.
U.S. stocks finished Wednesday's session in positive territory.
The S&P 500 jumped 1.31% to end the day at 7,619.38, while the Nasdaq Composite advanced 1.6% to close at 25,466.19. The Dow Jones Industrial Average gained 254.60 points, or 0.49%, to finish at 52,486.49.
Stocks can continue to climb on a broad basis, even if technology names lost ground, according to Goldman Sachs.
"One of the questions that has been permeating investor conversations this year is 'can the market go up if Tech goes down,'" a Goldman Sachs analyst wrote in a recent note to clients.  "While it's tempting to just say 'no,' November market price action provides a microcosm of the trade that suggests the answer may be 'yes.'"
The analyst noted that energy is the only sector in November that has underperformed info tech in the S&P 500 . Nevertheless, the broad-market index is still up 0.6% month to date.
The observation comes after the Nasdaq Composite slipped earlier this week, as losses in Nvidia led tech stocks lower.
Dan Niles, founder of Niles Investment Management, told CNBC's The Exchange on Wednesday that he doesn't think the market has hit the top of the AI trade, although he said he didn't know whether bear market conditions had materialized.
"I don't think it's the top for one simple reason: Agentic AI is very, very new," he said, touting the mass appeal of Meta's consumer AI product, Muse.
Asked about the possibility of a pullback in overall capex and equipment spending during the AI buildout, Niles said that such a scenario could present a problem for the market.
"If you're starting to pull back, then you've got an issue because now you're dealing with the other side of this, and in fact, it is March of 2000," he said, comparing the contingency he described to the popping of the dot-com bubble.
Even if the market enters a bear market, Niles said, it doesn't really matter for the way that he invests because investors can still play for strong positive rallies even as the overall trajectory is in decline.
Apple is set to close at another all-time high on Wednesday, two days after doing the same thing on Monday, when it finished the day at $350.69.
So far, the all-time intraday high of $355.38 reached last Thursday Nov. 5 remains unsurpassed.
Apple, the largest company in the U.S. with a market capitalization of some $5.1 trillion, has so far reached three all-time closing highs in November alone. The iPhone maker has soared 30.5% so far in 2026, nearly three times the 11.6% gain in the S&P 500.
Mortgage rates fell for four straight weeks, but that ended Tuesday, after a monthly inflation report came in hotter than expected. The average rate on the 30-year fixed mortgage rose 12 basis points from Monday to 7.30%, according to Mortgage News Daily. It was the largest one-day jump in more than a month.
Chicago Federal Reserve President Austan Goolsbee called the latest inflation data "borderline disturbing."
"It's another distressing report — borderline disturbing," Goolsbee said in an interview with the PBS NewsHour Tuesday.
"We've got a real inflation issue on our hands that has been developing," Goolsbee said. "We're going to have to deal with that."
The consumer price index rose 0.4% on a seasonally adjusted basis in October, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics' Tuesday morning release. That was higher than economists had predicted, and the third straight month of outsized price increases.
CoreWeave shares jumped 20% Wednesday after the neocloud posted quarterly earnings that beat estimates and raised its guidance for the year.
"Demand for the infrastructure is and remains overwhelming." CEO Michael Intrator told CNBC's "Squawk on the Street" Wednesday.
"I think I said that we are 10x oversubscribed to the existing capacity that we have left in 2027, and we are multiples ... oversubscribed on the capacity we have out in 2028," he said.
Berkshire Hathaway 's "Buffett premium" is evaporating, according to CFRA, citing "eroding fundamentals" and uncertainty around the "significant management transition."
In a Tuesday note, analyst Catherine Seifert highlighted insurance as a "weak spot" in during the firm's third quarter, which reported a decline in operating earnings .
She also mentioned shares of Berkshire "merit caution in the near term." At current levels, the stock trades at about 25 times CFRA's 2026 operating earnings per share, above their three-year average forward multiple of 23 times.
Warren Buffett announced his retirement as CEO at the end of 2025. He remains the chairman emeritus and a Board Director at the firm.
Current CEO Greg Abel, a CPA and the former CEO of MidAmerican Energy, brings "strong operational skills" to this role. Although, he still has big shoes to fill.
Still, Seifert highlighted bright spots, including Berkshire's balance sheet which continues to reflect "solid financial strength" as well as buybacks.
In Q3, the conglomerate bought back $9.6 billion worth of Berkshire stock.

articles.title_orig: Court Rules That Sexual Harassment Case Against SpaceX Can Proceed
articles.title_zh: Court Rules That Sexual Harassment Case Against SpaceX Can Proceed
articles.content_orig:
When a federal appeals court rejects a tech giant's bid to force a high-profile employment dispute into private arbitration, corporate legal teams take notice. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit recently delivered a striking 2-1 decision ruling that a lawsuit accusing SpaceX of illegal retaliation and sex discrimination must proceed in open court. For years, mandatory arbitration clauses have served as an invisible shield for powerful corporations, keeping employee complaints buried behind closed doors. This ruling cracks that shield open.
If you've been following how Silicon Valley handles internal dissent, this case marks a watershed moment. It highlights a widening chasm between executive behavior, corporate culture, and the statutory protections designed to protect workers who speak up.
The roots of this legal battle go back to a 2024 lawsuit filed by eight former SpaceX engineers. These employees circulated an internal open letter criticizing CEO Elon Musk, calling him a distraction and embarrassment while urging corporate leadership to formally distance themselves from provocative online commentary. Shortly after that letter made the rounds internally, SpaceX fired them.
The lawsuit claims that Musk's public statements and personal conduct fostered a pervasive, sexist atmosphere where female engineers routinely faced harassment and derogatory remarks. SpaceX has consistently denied these allegations, maintaining that the terminations were standard operational decisions rather than retaliatory measures.
Yet, the immediate battle wasn't about whether harassment happenedâit was about where the truth would come to light. SpaceX wanted the matter handled confidentially through private arbitration, a standard route that heavily favors employers by limiting public scrutiny, discovery depth, and media exposure. The engineers fought to keep the case in federal court, relying heavily on the federal Ending Forced Arbitration of Sexual Assault and Sexual Harassment Act (EFAA).
The legal mechanism at play here is just as important as the headline itself. Under the EFAA, individuals can bypass mandatory arbitration agreements if their cases involve sexual harassment or sexual assault disputes. SpaceX argued that the lawsuit primarily concerned wrongful termination and retaliation for criticizing the CEO, rather than an active sexual harassment dispute, meaning the arbitration waiver shouldn't apply.
The Ninth Circuit majority disagreed. By upholding the lower court's decision, the panel established that retaliation claims tied directly to raising sexual harassment concerns fall under the protective umbrella of the EFAA.
Writing in dissent, U.S. Circuit Judge Eric Tung warned that this interpretation opens the floodgates for disgruntled employees to manufacture sexual harassment claims simply to bypass binding arbitration agreements. But the majority held firm, ensuring that the plaintiffs can pursue their claims in the public sphere.
This creates a massive precedent. It signals to employers that you cannot easily silence internal whistleblowers by forcing them into private forums if the core grievance involves a sexually hostile work environment and subsequent retaliation.
Corporate accountability in the aerospace and technology sectors often hits a brick wall of NDAs and arbitration clauses. Elite engineering firms operate under intense pressure, where speed and output routinely overshadow internal cultural health. When executives project a culture that normalizes edgy or unfiltered commentary, it trickles down into everyday team dynamics.
When these disputes play out in open federal court rather than confidential arbitration rooms, the dynamics shift entirely. Discovery processes become public record. Internal emails, Slack messages, HR logs, and executive depositions face public scrutiny. That visibility changes how tech companies evaluate risk.
For workers, the ruling provides a clearer roadmap for utilizing federal statutes to challenge corporate retaliation. For leadership teams across Silicon Valley, it's a stark reminder that standard employment contracts and arbitration clauses are no longer foolproof armor against public employee lawsuits.
The case now returns to the lower court for standard pretrial litigation. While the plaintiffs still carry the burden of proving their allegations during trial, the hardest procedural hurdle has been cleared. The details of how SpaceX manages internal dissent and workplace culture will face an unfiltered public examination.

articles.title_orig: Why is gasoline suddenly under $4 a gallon?
articles.title_zh: Why is gasoline suddenly under $4 a gallon?
articles.content_orig:
AUSTIN, TEXAS - NOVEMBER 26: A gas pump is seen in a vehicle on November 26, 2025 in Austin, Texas. Brandon Bell/Getty Images hide caption
Stay up to date with our Up First newsletter, sent every weekday morning.
Drivers are starting to see some relief from high fuel prices. For the first time in months, the average price of a gallon of gasoline has dipped below $4, according to AAA .
The price crossed below the $4 threshold on Tuesday, and is currently down to a national average of $3.94 for a gallon of regular. Prices have dipped about 40 cents over the past month, with much of that decline happening in the past two weeks.
"Many will assume the election had something to do with it, but that's a myth," Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy, wrote in his industry newsletter .
Instead, he continued, gasoline prices are dropping for a more banal reason: "For now, it's the seasonal shift, not politics, driving the relief at the pump."
Gas prices often ease in the fall.
One reason: It's no longer summer, which is the peak season for gas. (Fewer people drive in colder weather, AAA points out .) With less demand, there's a touch more gas on the market.
Refineries also finish their annual maintenance by late fall. So that adds a bit more gas to go around.
And the blend of gasoline that's on the market gets cheaper.
Refineries make two types of gasoline every year: summer and winter blends. The summer blend produces less smog, because it evaporates less quickly in the heat; the winter blend helps engines start up in freezing weather, and uses a bit more butane, which helps lower its cost.
(Normally, the switch happens around September 15. This year, the Environmental Protection Agency and the Department of Energy said the switch would happen on September 1, citing gasoline prices that have been driven up by the war in Iran.)
But none of those are the biggest reason why gas prices are falling, says Jorge León, head of geopolitics at the research group Rystad Energy. The main driver is the falling price of Brent crude oil, which is now down to about $90 a barrel, and which is what refineries need to make gasoline, diesel and jet fuel.
That price is falling because there's a bit more oil coming out of the Middle East via pipelines, and because market traders have rejoiced at the intensifying diplomatic efforts between the U.S. and Iran.
That progress could easily be reversed if the war escalates, León wrote in an email to NPR. "President Trump may see further military action as a way to regain negotiating leverage before Democrats take control of Congress in January. If we see renewed escalation, much of last week's oil price decline could quickly reverse," he wrote. The same would be true for gas prices.
Congressional Democrats have expressed their support for ending the war in Iran. While they have limited power to do that, they do control the power of the purse, and can withhold additional war funding or hold back confirmations of key officials.
For now, if the price of Brent crude keeps falling, so could prices at the pump. "However, this does not mean a complete 'normalization,' a return to the price levels we had before this conflict started," Jaime Brito, executive director of refining and oil markets for Dow Jones Energy, wrote in an email to NPR.
To get back to pre-Iran war gas prices, the whole oil supply chain would have to recover. Ships that have been running long alternative routes to avoid the Strait of Hormuz would have to return to their points of origin, then resume their normal routes, taking crude oil to refineries. Those refineries would have to pump out enough fuel to alleviate global demand — and depleted stockpiles. The whole process could take months after a lasting peace deal.
"Coming back to those levels will require a return to normal crude production, shipping and refining of the entire global supply chain," Brito continued.
And while $4 a gallon may seem like a bargain these days, in an update on its website, AAA said that gasoline prices are still the highest they've ever been at this time of year.

articles.title_orig: Ukraine talks in Abu Dhabi bring progress on prisoners but not on peace
articles.title_zh: Ukraine talks in Abu Dhabi bring progress on prisoners but not on peace
articles.content_orig:
US envoys to visit Moscow and Dublin on Thursday for talks with Vladimir Putin and Volodymyr Zelenskyy respectively
Russia and Ukraine have agreed to the “largest prisoner exchange” of the war at their first US-brokered talks since February but made little progress towards a broader peace agreement.
Both sides sent senior delegations to the two-day talks, led by Donald Trump’s envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, in an effort to find a solution to end the nearly-five-year war.
David Arakhamia, a senior member of Ukraine’s delegation, said the Russian team had arrived with “very, very strict directives”, making it difficult to narrow differences. But he said there had been “really big progress” on security guarantees for Ukraine after the war. “I think we have good momentum to bring about a solution before the new year,” Arakhamia said.
Kushner, Trump’s son-in-law, also struck an upbeat tone, saying he could see a path to an agreement. “These deals are very hard and complex, and this one is very emotional, very complex. It’s a very hot war,” he said. “But we see all the different ingredients to make a deal. We just have to figure out how to refine those ingredients, organise them and create the right structure and pathway.”
Kushner said the planned exchange, expected to involve more than 1,000 prisoners from each side, would “reunite families, build trust and create momentum towards peace”.
The US envoys are due to travel to Moscow on Thursday to discuss the Abu Dhabi talks with Vladimir Putin, before heading to Dublin, where they are expected to meet Volodymyr Zelenskyy and a group of European partners.
“In close coordination with Ukraine and our European partners, we have aligned on proposals we will discuss with President Putin in Moscow tomorrow, followed by consultations with President Zelenskyy,” Kushner said.
But despite the optimism, Kushner also said the two sides had yet to resolve their territorial dispute.
Russia’s territorial demands have shifted over time, but Moscow has made clear it wants control of all the Donbas, including areas still held by Kyiv, as well as the parts of two southern regions it does not yet occupy.
Vladimir Medinsky, the hardline Russian official who led Moscow’s delegation, said that “every inch of our land will be returned to Russia, one way or another,” in a sign that Moscow was unwilling to soften its territorial demands. Russia would be satisfied with the negotiations only “when there is peace on its terms”, he added.
He also said the main task was to create a new security system in Europe that would become “a new Yalta and Potsdam”.
Medinsky said Europe’s post-second world war security system was failing, with Ukraine merely the place where its wider problems had erupted. “Essentially, the whole body is sick, and Ukraine was just a cyst that burst. The whole body must be cured. A Band-Aid won’t be enough,” Medinsky said.
His focus on Europe’s wider security order is likely to heighten concern among European leaders that Washington and Moscow could reach a broader agreement on the continent’s security, potentially limiting Nato’s military presence in eastern Europe. Russia appears to be seeking to revive demands it presented to Nato in 2021, including a halt to further enlargement that would rule out Ukraine’s membership, restrictions on Nato forces and weapons in European countries that joined after 1997, and limits on missile deployments.
That ultimatum was dismissed as a non-starter by the west and, weeks later, Russia invaded Ukraine .
Concerned that Europe’s security future could be discussed over their heads, European governments sent envoys to Abu Dhabi to try to influence the talks, although they are not believed to have taken part directly.
Medinsky dismissed their presence, saying that if they had come “as tourists”, they could talk in the hotel lobby, and that Russia would consider proposals only if they had “something specific” to offer.
European leaders have increasingly discussed the need for a direct channel to Putin , but no clear candidate has emerged. The leaders of Norway and Finland have recently spoken to the Russian president, while Germany’s chancellor, Friedrich Merz, said on Wednesday that he was open to doing so.
Kushner, meanwhile, said Europe should choose a single representative to speak on its behalf. “If Europe could identify one person to speak on their behalf, that would be a bigger achievement than getting the Russians to include them in the negotiations,” he said.
He stressed that one of the aims of his trip to Moscow was to “see if we can get Europeans added” to future talks. “The issues that were covered in these discussions were really postwar security,” he said. “How do we make sure that once this war ends, it doesn’t start again?”
Russian officials have long opposed European participation, arguing that countries supplying weapons to Kyiv cannot act as impartial mediators. Medinsky said Russia would speak to European countries only “when their conscience awakens” and they stop supplying Ukraine with weapons.
As diplomatic efforts continued, both sides kept up their attacks. Russia launched drones at Kyiv and other regions during the day, while Ukraine struck the Ust-Luga port on Russia’s Baltic coast overnight. The port, in the Leningrad region, is a major route for Russian energy exports and was still burning on Wednesday.

articles.title_orig: For Families of Those Who Died in the Iran War, a Veterans Day of Profound Loss
articles.title_zh: For Families of Those Who Died in the Iran War, a Veterans Day of Profound Loss
articles.content_orig:
This Armistice Day, CEO of OpenUK Amanda Brock argues that it is more important to regulate behaviour than technology.
This week marked Armistice Day, 11th November, when we wear poppies to commemorate the dead of the First and Second World Wars. We remember that they made the ultimate sacrifice for our freedom. Last Sunday, I was home in Crieff and saw the Remembrance parade. Wreaths were laid, as they were across the country, but it was the horses accompanying the procession that particularly stayed with me.
Over the summer, I saw War Horse at the National Theatre. It's a deeply moving story of a young man who enlists underage to find his beloved horse, Joey, after the horse is sold to the cavalry in the First World War. The contrast between the human relationships at the heart of the story and the increasingly technical and devastating reality of war was poignant. When British foot soldiers advanced at the Somme in July 1916, they faced machine-gun fire. By September, the British had introduced tanks into battle for the first time, in part to overcome the defences that had inflicted such heavy losses on them.
As told in the play, that began the technologisation of war. This process is one that has evolved over 100 years. Perhaps realistically it dates back to munitions and ammunition being developed. The turning point for the British forces as told in the play, what tipped the battle of the Somme, was the tank being rolled out by the British military, seeing the evolution of technology to fight technology.
A century later, warfare is still fought, but less through boots on the ground and increasingly shaped by technology, from drones and cyberattacks to AI-enabled intelligence and autonomous systems.
Ukraine has demonstrated how drones can change the balance of military power. Meanwhile, planes undertake emergency landings across Europe and fridges in the food supply chain are turned off – potentially by nation states . This disruption reminds us that the consequences of modern technological threats extend well beyond the battlefield.
In considering AI policy and regulation, we need to recognise the environment in which these technologies operate. Innovation can create both enormous opportunities and significant risks. The challenge is how to address those risks without unnecessarily restricting the technologies themselves.
Nick Clegg, now at Hiro Capital, has spoken this week about the disconnect between Big Tech, politics, and the willingness of these companies to express political opinion.
The same is true in reverse. A Baroness commented to me that she was shocked by how political - with a small p - tech is. That’s because the decisions on a word in a regulation is the difference between a loss and a billion-dollar revenue stream.
Neither sufficiently understands the other's world to make decisions that impact on the other. Yet decisions about technology increasingly shape almost every aspect of our lives and the delivery of our basic services. Hardly surprising when every aspect of our daily lives is reliant on technology today.
There is only one certainty in this digital world: we can only go forward, not back.
Of course, there’s much debate as to whether we regulate the underlying technology or how it is used. A bread knife can slice a loaf or be used as a weapon. We don't prohibit bread knives because they can cause harm; instead, we regulate harmful behaviour. The same distinction matters when considering general purpose technologies like AI. Generally we regulate use cases, and attempts to regulate coding per se would not be wise. We look to greater regulation in particular areas - regulated sectors - and that is appropriate.
The assumption that open source is inherently less secure persists, despite the evidence that security depends on far more than whether innovation is open or closed. Both forms have different challenges. Frankly, all technology has security challenges, and we need to consider what those are and how they are securely managed for a particular use case.
The Ukranians built drones on Arduino to use them in large-scale attacks. We see much of today’s warfare in Ukraine and in Iran being driven by technology. Ukraine's use of open source technologies in drone development illustrates how innovation can be adapted to meet urgent military needs. But the use of open technologies in warfare does not make the openness itself the problem. We need to distinguish between the technology, the people developing it and the purposes for which it is deployed.
What matters is how technology is developed, maintained, and deployed. Openness can support scrutiny that enables trust, but it is not a substitute for good security practice. The last conversation I had with Sir Alex Younger, former head of MI6, ended with him saying, with a smile, “May the open source be with you.” That followed a long discussion on why open source is not detrimental to security.
Regulators are challenged by complex technologies that evolve quickly. Those who understand the technologies are generally nowhere near the regulatory process.
Trust in AI remains a challenge in the West, and sensible regulation and policy has an important role to play in building it.
We must focus on addressing demonstrable risks, ensuring accountability and understanding how technologies are used, rather than treating innovation or openness as threats in themselves. To do this we need more of the right people in the room, bringing real technical understanding and building assurance.
In this world of geopolitical uncertainty good technological understanding in our policy has never mattered more.
